the next item is the report drawn up by mrs wallis on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, containing recommendations to the commission on limitation periods in crossborder disputes involving personal injury and death (2006/2014 (ini)) (a6-0405/2006).
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to thank mrs wallis for taking the initiative to harmonise the rules on the calculation of the number of hours worked and the limitation periods for personal injury claims in cross-border disputes. the further enlargement of the european union, the enrichment of societies, but also the freedom of movement, have all contributed to a significant increase in car traffic. unfortunately, this also increases the number of people injured in road accidents. currently, in national civil law systems, there are limitation periods ranging from very short, such as one year, to very long, such as 30 years. this is not conducive to the protection of victims, who often, unaware of the differences in limitation periods in different countries, bring actions for damages before foreign courts after the expiry of the limitation period. and then what happens? the court rejects the claim, and the injured party is left without the possibility of asserting his rights. the unification would help to introduce certain and transparent rules which would enable both victims of accidents and their representatives, whose situation i know very well as a lawyer, to pursue their claims. that is why i fully support this initiative.
mr. chairman, please! first of all, i would like to thank very much mrs. diana wallis for the work she has done. i remember the special meetings that she initiated in the legal affairs committee so that we could get to know this issue - an issue of great importance to all citizens of the european union. i cannot agree with the commissioner that the simple explanation for the laziness or delay in this legislative initiative is the formal impossibility of interfering with national legal systems. every time i take the floor here and have the opportunity to do so, i remind you that the primary duty of any parliament, of any institution with the power to legislate, is to create a law that is simple, clear and serves the citizens, a law that makes their lives easier. if today we are dealing with 27 different legal systems with regard to limitation periods for property claims related to various types of accidents, it is our duty - both of the european parliament, the european commission and the council - to find a way to change this situation and to create a law that makes life easier. because it is difficult to explain to any victim or to the family of the person who has died that formally everything has long been closed: that we can only feel sorry for her, and that the lawsuits that have been filed after the expiry of the limitation period can only be dismissed. i therefore ask the european commission to try to take all possible measures and to obtain the legislative competence to regulate this matter. i am deeply convinced that there is an understanding in the member states that this very issue, which affects hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of citizens of the european union, needs a quick and good solution. if we want to maintain the activity of union citizens which is linked to movement between countries, we must also support it with such solutions.
mr. president, i would like to thank you for your service. i would like to begin by congratulating ms wallis on her contribution to the european parliament's draft resolution. it is true that there are currently considerable differences in the european union in terms of the time limits for crossborder disputes involving injuries and fatalities. as the rapporteur has rightly pointed out, the problem in this case is complex and concerns both the limitation period and the start of the period, the limitation period, the time limit for becoming aware of the event, the possibility of suspending or stopping the period, and the taking of evidence and the lodging of a statement of opposition to the limitation period. a high degree of disparity can have adverse effects on accident victims, often making it difficult for them to enforce their rights through the courts. ensuring legal certainty for all citizens of the european union and facilitating the exercise of the freedoms provided for in the treaties is a priority. i therefore ask the committee to submit a legislative proposal to the european parliament which should take account of the pertinent recommendations attached to the draft resolution.
mr. chairman, please! i just wanted to congratulate ms. wallis on a great and much-needed report that meets the needs of victims of various accidents. you have rightly stressed that the union is open to its citizens, who can travel and move freely, but unfortunately there is a risk of accidents. their victims often suffer twice, once because of the accidents and the second time because of ignorance of the laws of the country where they were injured, resulting in statute of limitations and the inability to pursue legitimate claims. the proposal to introduce a minimum limitation period for crossborder claims uniform throughout the union is therefore to be fully supported. it is a proposal that protects victims, increases their ability to exercise their rights and as such deserves our full support. i hope that the commission will follow up this report by putting forward proposals for concrete solutions which take account of the well-being of people who have been harmed by the events of the past.

member of the commission. mr president, the issue of security of supply is of particular importance for the european union and a number of events over the past few years highlight the need for the european union to reinforce its policy measures in this area. let us remember the wake-up call we had last year between russia and ukraine and this year between russia and belarus. i would like to try to provide you today with a short summary of the different initiatives that the commission has taken to increase our security of supply in general, and in particular in the relationship with the russian federation. energy supplies from the russian federation play an important role in meeting europe’s energy needs, accounting for nearly 30% of the eu’s oil imports and 44% of our gas imports. at the same time, 67% of russia’s oil and gas exports are delivered to the european market and, given the mutual importance of this relationship, an energy dialogue was established in 2000 between the russian federation and the eu to discuss energy-related issues, including energy policy, market developments, infrastructure and eu-russia energy cooperation on technology and energy efficiency. in addition, there is a roadmap for the common economic space that was agreed during the eu-russia summit in may 2005, and that includes cooperation on wide-ranging issues of energy and related activities. moreover, a new agreement is to be negotiated with the russian federation to follow on from the existing eu-russia partnership and cooperation agreement which expires at the end of the year. it is now intended that this will include a comprehensive agreement on energy. let me also point out that in the recent communication, ‘an energy policy for europe’, the commission formulated quite a number of proposals to mitigate our growing dependence on external energy supplies and to increase our energy security. the commission underlines that there is no singular solution, but there has to be a variety of different initiatives that must be pursued. they include increased energy efficiency, promotion of renewable energy sources, the diversification of energy supplies, proper functioning of the internal market and internal solidarity mechanisms to cope with possible supply interruptions, including through cooperation with the international energy agency. furthermore, the importance of strengthening our relations with all our key energy suppliers and transit countries and for the eu to speak with a single voice is also underlined in the communication. in response to recent interruptions in the energy supply field from russia through belarus, the commission also convened meetings earlier this year of both the gas coordination group and the oil support group, which comprised, inter alia, representatives of the member states. these meetings to which the third countries concerned were invited to give information then reviewed the impact on the eu’s internal energy security of the events in question and how to respond. finally, with reference to the area of strengthening energy dialogue, the commission is committed to maintaining and to reinforcing our energy relations, not only with the russian federation, but also with other important energy-producing countries and regions like norway, the countries of the opec, the gulf cooperation council, the countries of the caspian and the black sea basins, central asia and north africa through bilateral agreements and energy dialogues.

member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr gahler and his colleagues for this report. the commission is convinced that, in order to strengthen the capacity of governments to plan and implement macroeconomic, sectoral and public finance reforms, and to stimulate growth and alleviate poverty, budget support can be more effective than other types of support, provided that certain eligibility conditions are met, and i want to stress this caveat, provided that certain eligibility conditions are met. budget support provides financing in relation to capital costs and current expenditure necessary to achieve the millennium development goals, such as the construction of schools, hospitals or roads, the payment of teachers, nurses, the maintenance of infrastructure, etc. on the other hand, by providing support to the budget of a country rather than to a specific project, not only are transaction costs reduced, but the accountability of local authorities in relation to the use of funds is also strengthened, provided that there is a mechanism for monitoring the use of these funds in the recipient countries themselves, and that is one of the elements of the conditionality or eligibility conditions to which i referred earlier. experience over the past few years shows that budget support can - and indeed often does - meet these expectations. this is corroborated by the clearly positive assessment last year by the oecd development assistance committee of general budget support in seven countries analysed by that committee. we therefore welcome the comments in mr gahler's report on budget support as an essential instrument of development cooperation in the european union. this was also reflected in the european consensus on development adopted last year. this consensus, this joint declaration by parliament, the council and the commission, commits us to increasing budget support where conditions allow. we are working intensively with member states and other bodies to ensure that this commitment is fulfilled, in full respect of the legal framework already in place. it is necessary, however, to answer a question mentioned in mr gahler's report, but which, in our opinion, does not entirely correspond to reality. because, according to our analysis, budget support is not synonymous with recklessness or mismanagement, but rather the opposite. the commission applies strict eligibility criteria when selecting which countries should receive budget support. such criteria are reassessed before each disbursement under the general support programme. the aim is to minimise the risk of budget support being wasted or to try to prevent it being used in an inappropriate way. improving public financial management is also a key objective of our budget support. our approach is to assess the direction and credibility of the public financial management reforms that our assistance can support, rather than to demand that specific minimum standards be met. this approach is shared by other budget support bodies and was not challenged in the court of auditors' 2005 special report, whose main recommendations the commission has taken into account in developing a revised set of guidelines for budget support. we fully agree with the call in the report to consolidate the institutions which play a key role in the control of the executive, but we believe that these institutions should be national, responding to the local political framework, and not foreign bodies which are accountable to donors. in general, the commission considers that good governance, which is crucial for development, cannot be imposed from outside. the establishment of innovative partnerships, conceived in accordance with the governance initiative and the commission's communication on this subject, is a promising way of promoting good governance. finally, while the positive conclusions of the recent independent evaluations of budget support are encouraging, we agree on the need to continuously assess the effectiveness of budget support and to ensure that the results are clearly disseminated, in order to build public support for development cooperation.

mr. chairman, please! first of all, i would like to congratulate mr michael gahler on his report on budgetary aid to developing countries. in recent years, budgetary assistance has become the leading form of eu development aid. for the european commission, it is the main instrument of community development policy. indeed, in favourable circumstances, budgetary assistance can be a powerful tool to help achieve the european union's objectives of development aid, sustainable economic and social development, the smooth and gradual integration of developing countries into the world economy, the fight against poverty, economic and employment growth, and the development and consolidation of democracy. in the european parliament's report, we stress that budget support as an instrument of assistance can only be effective if both partners take full responsibility in a true spirit of partnership. parliament called for budget support to be concentrated as much as possible on development priorities relating to poverty reduction, for these to be given a central role in the policy dialogue between donor and recipient, and for parliamentary scrutiny to be guaranteed on both donor and recipient sides. the rule of law, democracy and decentralisation are, in our view, the best guarantees for the proper use of development funds.
mr. chairman, please! the activities of the european investment bank for 2005 were positively assessed by the rapporteur and i would like to share that assessment. the institution has been working for some time to implement projects in line with the lisbon strategy and i believe that the positive effects of these projects will be felt in the near future. nevertheless, i would like to make a few comments on the eib's activities. first, i would like to point out that the eib's primary objective is to promote the economic and social cohesion of the countries of the european union. a significant part of the bank's funds should therefore be concentrated in the poorest regions of the european union. however, as the author of the report rightly noted, over the last four years, including 2005, we have seen a reversal of proportions. the regions receiving the most support were those covered by objective 2, rather than the less economically developed objective 1 regions. secondly, there is a clear tendency for the eib to support the southern regions of the european union at the expense of its eastern regions. the same applies to non-eu countries. while the bank has many projects in the so-called mediterranean neighbourhood, i could not find a single project in the eastern neighbourhood on the eib's website. the last point concerns the evaluation of the effectiveness of the projects carried out by the bank. it is clear to me that the eib should evaluate its performance ex post by measuring it against economic growth and employment growth. in particular, i agree with the rapporteur that the provision and analysis of information on failed projects can provide guidance to the bank in its decision to pursue projects in the future.

mr. chairman, please! i am aware that the concept of corporate social responsibility is becoming an increasingly important part of the debate on globalisation, competitiveness and sustainable development. by definition, companies are voluntarily taking social and environmental issues into account in their activities. in the exercise of their social responsibility on a voluntary basis, companies choose to go beyond minimum legal requirements and collective agreements to take account of social and environmental needs. i would like to emphasize very clearly that it is the application of the principle of voluntariness in the approach to implementation, to the participation of enterprises in the concept of social responsibility, that is crucial. as csr is based primarily on the voluntary decision of companies, i believe that any additional administrative obligations and requirements would most likely have the opposite effect and would be contrary to the principles of better regulation and the better and simpler functioning of the european union. i have expressed this by submitting ten amendments to the text proposed by mr howit and i am glad that the spirit of these amendments is reflected in the compromise text proposed by the rapporteur. i would also like to emphasise the importance of using the method of exchanging good practice in implementing the concept of corporate social responsibility. in practice, this is possible within the framework of the european alliance for corporate social responsibility and i would like to acknowledge the commitment of the european commission, which, recognising that it is companies that are the main actors on this stage, declares its support for the functioning of this platform, which is a good, open form of exchange of good practices by large, medium and small companies alike.

member of the commission. mr president, it gives me great pleasure to be able to present to you the new eu consumer policy strategy for 2007-2013, adopted today by the commission. i see this as our contribution to making every citizen safe and confident everywhere in the union. i hope this house will give its support to this goal. this is also our contribution to increasing the economic wellbeing of our citizens and the competitiveness of the eu economy. i know the importance of consumer policy to parliament and welcome the support that has been given to consumer policy in the past. your support for my nomination as commissioner for consumer policy clearly indicated your expectations of the commission, and i trust the strategy will be in line with your priorities. what is important for the consumer financial programme 2007-2013, in relation to which parliament has been a key actor in the legislative process in terms of ensuring the smooth adoption of that programme? the programme is an important tool for the delivery of the strategy, and the changes made in the programme to take account of your views have also been factored into the strategy. the strategy and, indeed, my appointment as the first commissioner for consumer affairs are the beginnings of a response to the vision of this parliament. some of you have been calling for a stronger consumer dimension to all eu policies for some time now. consumer policy seems to me to be equally well placed to tackle the two big challenges the eu faces today: boosting growth and jobs, and reconnecting with our citizens. on growth and jobs, it is clear that the internet is fundamentally changing the retail sector, but these changes have, in practice, so far been limited to national markets. on the retail side of the internal market, we see fragmentation into 27 national mini-markets, and this is both a pity and a missed opportunity as the internal market has the potential to be the largest retail market in the world, with significant benefits to consumers and to the competitiveness of the eu economy. opening up cross-border retail is the key to unlocking the full potential of the internal market. if cross-border shopping becomes a credible alternative to domestic shopping, then competitive pressure will increase, not only in cross-border shopping but also in domestic retail markets. the integration effect does not require all, or even most, consumers to do most of their shopping across borders. our experience in removing obstacles to the cross-border sale of new vehicles shows that it is enough for cross-border shopping to be a credible alternative for competition to be enhanced in the domestic markets. this would be good for growth and jobs. however, we need a strategy that also responds directly to the aspirations of all our citizens. for them, an active consumer policy should be a central part of our efforts to show that they can improve their daily lives by taking advantage of opportunities created by europe in terms of broader markets, lower prices and guaranteed rights and protection. putting consumers at the heart of all eu policies and regulations is important. this is not just about a narrow consumer policy strip of european policy; the strategy commits us all, in parliament as well as in the commission, to look harder at all eu policies to be sure that we have properly taken account of the impact of consumers and have adjusted policies to maximise their benefits. president barroso has therefore decided to expand the mandate of the competitiveness group of commissioners to address the consumer dimension so that all proposals with a significant impact on consumers will in future undergo closer scrutiny. under our consumer policy, we see three main objectives over the next seven years. first, i want to empower europe’s consumers. this means creating the right market conditions for them to be able to make informed, considered and original choices and equipping them with the tools to do so. second, i want to enhance the economic and non-economic welfare of europe’s consumers in terms of price, choice, quality and affordability. third, i want to protect consumers effectively. market failures for consumers fall into two categories – those that individuals cannot address and those that they should address themselves. consumer laws should effectively protect consumers from the former and equip them to deal with the latter. in short, i want the commission to be able to tell all eu citizens by 2013 that they can shop anywhere in the eu, from the corner shop to the website, confident that they are equally effectively protected and to be able to tell all retailers that they can sell anywhere on the basis of a single, simple set of rules. we are a long way from those goals now. important progress has been made, with the help of the european parliament: the directive on unfair commercial practices, the regulation on consumer protection cooperation and the network of european consumer centres have made significant progress. we need to complete this work and act on a number of fronts: better rules on contracts, better enforcement, information, advice and redress all need to work as well in the internal market as at home if consumers and smes are to be persuaded to make this leap. harmonised rules in targeted areas are central to an integrated market – but not to keep lawyers and bureaucrats happy. a simple clear set of rules helps smes, consumers and enforcers, and i am not sure it is possible to encourage consumers and smes to see the eu market as a truly single territory without simple rules, but harmonised rules will not create this necessary increase in current levels of consumer confidence if harmonisation is agreed in a way that provides inadequate substantive levels of protection. my preference is for harmonised rules and good protection. this commission has recently launched an important consultation in this area and i welcome parliament’s opinion on these matters. in conclusion, in such a short time i can only give a brief flavour of the strategy. i think it sets out an ambitious agenda and on that we will require parliament’s support in order for it to be successfully delivered.

on behalf of the uen group. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: i welcome the opening of the debate on the reform of the european union's trade policy instruments. the current system of trade defence instruments, which has remained unchanged for the past dozen or so years, is no longer sufficiently effective to counteract the negative effects of increasing globalisation. since the problem is too vast to be discussed in detail here, i would like to draw attention to the issues that should be changed. first, the basis for the commission to impose anti-dumping duties on imports of a product is to show that its price on the union market does not exceed its cost of production. the commission therefore primarily examines the prices of the factors of production, e.g. wages, prices of materials, energy, etc., and does not examine whether the entrepreneur bears the costs of social security contributions for employees or whether he bears the costs of complying with environmental protection standards. it is thus difficult to conclude that the costs quoted are incomplete and thus the price of the product which does not include them is artificially undercutting the price. secondly, very often the relatively high prices of some products originating in the union and thus the lack of competitiveness on the world market are due to the need to meet very high standards, for example in terms of animal welfare. the european union should require that such products brought into the european union market from third countries also meet such standards. thirdly, the european commission is very cautious about the application of so-called safeguard clauses, which are intended to protect the union market against a sudden flood of the union market by a given type of product. however, this instrument is much faster and easier to use than anti-dumping duties. finally, fourthly, the commission should also endeavour to reduce to the minimum necessary the time between the initiation of the procedure and the implementation of the trade defence instrument concerned. at present, this period is several months, for example, in the case of anti-dumping duties, up to nine months, which exposes european producers to huge losses.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank all the speakers for their very constructive contributions to this afternoon’s discussion. first of all, i would like to repeat that from the conservation point of view there is no basis to take any action, because in 1970s we had 2 million seals of the most hunted species, and now we have 5.8 million of these seals. we are looking only at the second issue – it is very important. as regards the study, firstly i have to repeat that the commission fully recognises the high level of public concern regarding the application of humane killing methods, and in line with its commitment to high animal welfare standards, we will examine all available information. there are reports – which are partly contradictory – that seals are being hunted and killed in some regions in an inhumane way. the assessment that i referred to – and which one of the speakers found to be necessary – will present balanced, objective and operational conclusions and recommendations. the overall outcome should enable the commission to draw some conclusions and to come back with possible legislative proposals if this is warranted by the situation. regarding the moratorium, in legal terms the commission does not have available an immediate remedy to impose a moratorium on the import, export and trade in seal products. it would not be possible to refer to the safeguard measures provided for under the public health and animal policy that would allow for a temporary ban when public or animal health is threatened. for example, the decision to temporarily suspend imports of wild birds was adopted in order to protect animal and public health because of the risk of a worldwide spread of avian influenza. furthermore, under the trade policy there is no immediate remedy possible. any measure the european union decided to adopt would need to be necessary and proportional and would need to be notified to the world trade organization. at this stage it is therefore not appropriate, nor is it feasible, to impose an immediate trade ban. the commission first needs to carry out an objective assessment of all available information. the outcome of this assessment should enable the commission to draw sound conclusions and to come back with possible legislative proposals if this is warranted by the situation. reference was made to the united states, and its marine mammal protection act was enacted in 1972, which was before the international convention on trade in endangered species entered into force in 1975. furthermore, member states have the opportunity to impose measures according to the case law of the european court of justice, but the community has no such legal basis. i would ask you to urge your governments in your member states to impose bans – they have the legal means. we need to have the appropriate legal basis before we can impose bans at european union level and that is what we are trying to do by having an impact assessment and by gathering information. however, if you show your concern in your countries and urge your governments to impose bans, this will facilitate internal market reasons for the european union to take steps. finally, i wish to reiterate that the commission is strongly committed to high animal welfare standards, both within the european union and at international level. a full objective assessment of the animal welfare aspects of seal hunting will allow us to see the whole picture and have a solid basis before drawing any conclusions. we shall examine all available information and take the necessary steps. if it is established that seals are being hunted and killed in an inhumane way, a ban on the import and export, as well as the placing of products derived from the seal hunt on the market, will also be considered. we will report back to the european parliament within the shortest possible time. i repeat that we have already asked the european food safety authority to conduct the scientific part of the study, and i have written to the canadian government to ask that we be allowed to participate in a mission, and the european parliament is also invited to participate in order to see how the hunt is being organised. what you said previously about your experiences is very interesting.

the next item is the report drawn up by mr zingaretti on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights on the amended proposal for a european parliament and council directive on criminal law measures aimed at ensuring the enforcement of intellectual property rights (com ((2006) 0168 c6-0233/2005 2005/0127 cod)) (a6-0073/2007).
mr. chairman, please! the directive on criminal measures for the enforcement of intellectual property rights represents a reversal of the commission's approach to criminal law. the proposed document reflects the interpretation of the european court of justice judgment of 12 september 2005 adopted by the european commission, which allows for the application of criminal sanctions at community level where they are necessary for the effective implementation of union law. in view of the growing problem of intellectual property infringement worldwide, the approach proposed by the commission seems not only appropriate but also necessary. the european union's gdp is shrinking by about €8 billion a year because of counterfeiting. individual companies lose between 45 and 65 billion euros every year because of this. the scale of the problem is so great that it is estimated that about 40 percent of the world's computer software is derived from illegal sources, as are 36 percent of the world's cds and music cassettes. in view of the above, it is welcome that in the case of serious crimes committed within criminal organisations, the maximum penalty can be up to eur 300 000 and/or 4 years of imprisonment. it should also be noted that, according to parliament's proposal, criminal measures will only be applied to entities and persons who commit intentional infringements for commercial purposes. it is very important to note that the directive does not cover infringements of the above property rights by private users who are not motivated by a desire to make a profit. moreover, it seems justified to exclude the proposed patent law directive from its scope, which will avoid any prejudice as to the content of future legislation on this matter and will limit the scope of the directive in question to intellectual property rights only. finally, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr zingaretti, on a very well-drafted document.
mr. chairman, please! contrary to what some of my colleagues in this chamber are saying, the proposal for a directive was made in response to the growing practice of intellectual property theft. we are well aware that current eu law does not provide for a community policy to punish piracy and counterfeiting. the commission rightly notes that the differences between the systems used by the member states are too great. this obviously makes it difficult to protect intellectual property effectively, and this in turn has a direct negative impact on the value of innovation investments. i am convinced that it is essential to combat this practice at community level. and when we realize that counterfeit products, such as drugs and toys, can be dangerous to our health and lives, the problem becomes even more serious. it is obvious that to counterfeit any product requires additional packaging, graphic designers, distributors, etc., so one person cannot do it. this is the work of more or less organised criminal groups, and it is these groups that the directive is intended to target in particular. the solutions proposed in the draft directive should be considered as favourable. infringement of intellectual property rights is a crime and must be punished. but there is a debate about the limits of responsibility, and more importantly, who is responsible. those who produce and market counterfeit goods should be held absolutely accountable. it would be unacceptable to punish those who have acquired or used goods or services without knowing their illegal origin. the commission proposal does not define intentional conduct clearly enough in the context of intellectual property infringements and this needs to be corrected. in conclusion, the adoption of the text of the directive is a necessary step, and it is only to be regretted that we cannot afford another one today. it is possible to identify groups of crimes that are particularly difficult to combat effectively in a globalised world, based on dozens of different legal systems. i believe that greater harmonisation of criminal law in the european union would greatly improve this efficiency, and the course of today's debate confirms this.

the next item is the report drawn up by mr janusz wojciechowski on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (ec) no 1868/94 establishing a quota system for the production of potato starch (com ((2006) 0827 - c6-0046/2007 - 2006/0268 (cns)) (a6-0137/2007).
member of the commission. mr president, i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr wojciechowski, and members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for the work that has been carried out on this report. i shall start by placing this proposal in its context. since the potato starch production quotas were introduced back in 1995, we have been trying to define a strategy that could secure, enhance and promote the development of this important sector. however, over the last decade the european union’s agricultural policies have changed dramatically, becoming more market-oriented with the decoupling of most aid payments, and reforms of the market organisations in almost all sectors. in spite of the existence of quotas, potato starch production exceeds demand on the european market with the result that we have to export about 40% of our production into the world market, usually with the benefit of export refunds. concerning the proposals that we are discussing today, it is of vital importance to preserve the stability of this very fragile sector while at the same time taking the fundamental changes due to the reform of the common agricultural policy into account. the main objectives of the proposals are firstly to roll over the quotas for another two years, which will allow us to review the potato starch system in the framework of the health check. an extension of four years, as you propose in your report, would not allow us to take the opportunity to go into details with this important sector in the health check, and therefore you will understand that we cannot accept this amendment. the second main objective is to roll over the existing quotas, which have actually provided a relatively stable market for potato starch in the european union. i am aware that there have been repeated requests from some member states for an increase in their quotas, and i have not forgotten the declaration made by the council. however, an analysis of the current market situation has shown that an increase of the potato starch production quotas should be avoided at the moment. if we increase the quotas in a situation where we have over-production within the european union, this would put even heavier pressure on the prices. we should take the opportunity to take another two years as suggested, and then, in the health check, go into details to see what a viable future for our potato starch production could look like.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. this is the fifth time that the european parliament has considered a regulation on potato starch production quotas. i have the honour to report on this regulation for the second time. i had the pleasure of meeting you in 2005. in practice, we have two issues to resolve. firstly, for how long the system of limiting potato starch production is to be extended and, secondly, whether the production quotas allocated to individual countries are to be maintained unchanged or adjusted. the european commission proposes to maintain the quota system for another 2 years without any change in the amounts. however, in the committee on agriculture, many meps pointed out that two years was far too short for any sensible planning and the commission therefore adopted a four-year period. as rapporteur, i supported this proposal. and it's right, because farmers and starch producers can't be surprised by too much change too quickly. the question of the production quotas for starch is more difficult. the two new member states, poland and lithuania, indicate, as they did two years ago, that the amounts allocated to them are too low in relation to their potential and needs. lithuania has a quota of around 1200 tonnes and cannot maintain even one plant, as a consequence lithuania has stopped producing starch, but wants and needs to produce within 4,7 thousand tonnes. poland, the largest potato producer in europe, or more precisely in the european union, received 144 thousand tonnes, several times less than the largest german, french and dutch quotas. as rapporteur, i proposed an increase in the quotas for poland and lithuania, totalling less than 40 000 tonnes, which is less than 2% of the total quota of 1948 000 tonnes. however, by a margin of 17 votes to 20, the proposal to increase the amounts was rejected in committee. as rapporteur, i have a duty to present the arguments of the majority, which is small. it is also my duty to mention the reasons of the minority which has tabled its amendments. the committee was concerned that the increase in quotas could destabilize the market. i think that's an unwarranted concern. first, it is a small increase, less than 2% of the total. second, the market has changed. potato starch, although of better quality, is replaced by inferior grain starch. the proportion of potato starch in total production has decreased over the last 3 years from 25% to 20%. it means there's just no potato starch. thirdly, there is a disproportion between the old and the new member states. the old countries have 90% of the quota and the new ones only 10%, although they represent more than 25% of the union's population potential. fourthly, the amounts allocated are often not used, by a few or even a dozen percent. if a crop fails, the market is short of starch and this is not compensated for in subsequent years, beyond the allowable balancing within the limits of 5% of the amount. fifthly, the fact that poland and lithuania are being disadvantaged by the quota system is not even disputed by the european commission, which two years ago, through the very mouth of the commissioner present here, mrs fisher boel, promised to take account of the special situation of these two countries, and nothing of the sort has happened. sixthly and lastly, in the face of the obvious needs of the two member states, which are clearly harmed by the current system, european solidarity is needed, not european egoism. the accession negotiations concluded certain matters five years ago, but that does not mean that we should be their eternal hostage and that we should turn a blind eye to the economic changes that have occurred since then. high isbo! in closing, i would like to draw attention to amendment 8, which may be the basis of a good compromise. its meaning is that if in one year there were any unused amounts in the whole system, then in the following year the member states concerned, but only the new ones, could ask the commission to grant additional amounts within the limits of the unused amounts in the previous year. in this way, actual production settled over a multiannual period would not exceed the 1948 thousand tonnes ceiling and the new member states would be able to apply for higher amounts. i'm asking you to consider accepting this amendment, which could lead to a good compromise.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. this is the second debate in the european parliament on the potato starch quota during the current term of the next item is the report drawn up by mr antolína sánchez presedo on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy on the green paper: claims for compensation for the use of restrictive practices and abuse of a dominant position (2006/2207 (ini)) ().
member of the commission. mr president, honourable members, we are here tonight to debate an issue of fundamental importance: rights. the court has been clear: the right to damages is necessary to guarantee the effectiveness of community competition rules. but consumers and business customers do not use their rights. injuries are left uncompensated, while society and the economy absorb the loss: that is just reality. that is clearly unjust, incompatible with our community of law and at odds with our shared competitiveness objectives. the european commission and, i believe, most members of this house will not tolerate this situation. our green paper set out the problems. finding appropriate solutions requires a very careful, measured approach, grounded in european legal traditions and developed through dialogue with stakeholders and, in particular, with parliament. that is why the commission will present a white paper, accompanied by an impact assessment, for further discussion around the new year. mr sánchez presedo’s report provides a wealth of pertinent input into this process. i congratulate the rapporteur wholeheartedly and thank the shadow rapporteurs and the committee on economic and monetary affairs for all their work. i also thank mr doorn and the members of the committee on legal affairs for their contribution. we will give most careful consideration to all parliament’s recommendations in preparing the white paper. i am aware that some are concerned that fostering private damage actions might lead to a us-style litigation culture. we will certainly take this into account in drafting the white paper. but the scales are currently tipped against the victims. carefully balanced european solutions need to be found. common solutions that meet the strict tests of proportionality and subsidiarity should only be developed where national rules do not guarantee the right to damages effectively. i have also heard it said that more private actions will create additional costs for business. we heard similar arguments years ago as regards the ‘polluter pays’ principle for the environment. the fact is that today cartels and other abuses cause huge but hidden costs. empirical research shows that international cartels raise prices by over 20%. recent cartel decisions by the commission covered synthetic rubber, gas-insulated switch gear and acrylic glass. all these cartels increased input costs for business and harmed european competitiveness. the time has come to introduce the ‘competition-infringer pays’ principle. let us not forget that, whilst some industries have to create some pollution to do business, in the competition environment there is no need and no excuse for infringements. infringers may not like having to repair the damage they cause, but they should simply not break the rules in the first place. it is their choice. i believe that making sure businesses and consumers do not lose out because of the illegal behaviour of some companies is worth fighting for. i sincerely hope that this week parliament will send a strong message of support for this objective. we will discuss the detail together later, on the basis of a white paper that will be balanced and measured and subject to the vigorous and very valuable scrutiny of this house.
member of the commission. mr president, honourable members, over 40 years ago in van gend & loos, the court gave eu market players and citizens the rights they need to play a central role in our european project. the legal environment in which the victims of antitrust infringements currently find themselves is not acceptable. i got the message that everybody agrees on that. i would like to thank you for the stimulating debate here this evening on how we might gradually improve this legal environment, and i look forward to parliament’s vote on the report. so far, so good. i would now like to respond to a few issues raised in our debate this evening. mr doorn raised the question of legal base. that is important and quite clear. at the stage of a green paper, and in the absence of any commission proposal, it is rather premature, if you will allow me to say so, to discuss the question of legal base at this stage. the treaty offers appropriate, specific and general legal bases for measures in this area and i imagine that we could agree upon that. however, a pertinent base, and hence the applicable procedure, can only be identified in line with the nature, objectives and scope of any individual measure possibly envisaged after the white paper. i will, however, consider the extent to which it may be appropriate to say something about legal bases in the forthcoming white paper. so, there is still something to look at there. i am aware of the need to be sensitive as regards national procedural rules. there is no doubt about that. that is quite a clear warning. on substance, we already have one uniform european competition law, and by their very nature, breaches of the antitrust rules have a cross-border impact because they affect our internal market, and that is what we are protecting. it makes sense to me that the right to compensation should also be equally enforceable throughout our internal market. it is only to the extent that the procedural rules of the member states do not guarantee effectively the substantive rights conferred by the treaty that the commission may seek some approximation of these rules. any measures proposed would have to meet the strict tests of subsidiarity, proportionality and necessity. the white paper will be accompanied by an impact assessment, as i have already said. mr evans mentioned the need to avoid encouraging a litigation culture and the risk of unmerited claims being brought. the commission is encouraging a competition culture compatible with our existing european legal cultures. we will pursue a measured and balanced approach, because like you, we are determined to avoid opening the door to the excesses which some other jurisdictions have experienced. but fear is a very bad adviser. none of the key characteristics of us antitrust litigation is suggested as an option in the green paper. many of those of support facilitating damage actions, like mrs bowles, stressed the need to avoid tilting the scales too much in favour of claimants. however, these same commentators also recognised that the scales are currently tipped against the victims of antitrust damages, and hence that something should be done. the commission is striving for a proportionate and measured approach developed in consultation with stakeholders. mrs wallis mentioned collective actions for damages claims. given the costs of litigation, it is unlikely that individual consumers will bring small-value damages claims against the perpetrators of competition law infringements. so it is worth looking at options for collective redress, as she rightly mentioned. the green paper looks at representative actions brought by consumer organisations. so let us be clear – and i repeat – us-style opt-out class actions are not on the agenda and will not be on my agenda. in opt-out class actions, lawyers act on behalf of an unidentified class of persons and mainly pursue their own interests. in representative actions, the latter have no separate interest different from that of the injured parties they represent. the commission thus believes that the interests of consumers are better served by a representative action than by an opt-out class action, and i hope this will also reassure mrs berès. your involvement signals the importance of the debate launched by the green paper, and is a reason for hope, as we are all aware that there is something to be done. there is no doubt about it: the devil is in the detail. i should like to leave you with two key messages. first, i hope that this house will send out a strong signal that the current situation is not acceptable and that is what i have got from you. this is all about rights, and this house has been a consistent supporter of rights across all policies and all areas of european cooperation. we have to give european citizens and european businesses the ability to exercise their rights under european competition laws. this is an area in which the community can show its relevance to the daily life of citizens and to business. second, it is by working together in dialogue, through ideas and constructive criticism, that we will be able to make improvements, at the same time avoiding the known pitfalls. i look forward to taking this process forward with the white paper at the turn of the year. thank you for the interesting debate and thank you especially, rapporteur, for your hard work on this important file.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on wednesday at 12 noon.

member of the commission. the experience gained from the application of regulation (ec) no 2204/2002 is currently being used by the commission in order to establish revised rules applying to aid for employment of disabled workers in the context of the preparation of a new commission regulation, which will revise, consolidate, simplify and harmonise the existing block exemption regulations. this new regulation, which forms part of the implementation of the state aid action plan, will replace existing instruments, including regulation (ec) no 2204/2002. the commission adopted a first draft of the regulation just today. this will allow the commission to consult member states and listen to the views of other interested stakeholders, including the european parliament, in the coming months, in line with the procedure established by council regulation (ec) no 994/98 on the application of articles 92 and 93 of the treaty establishing the european community to certain categories of horizontal state aid. block exemption regulations only apply to measures which constitute state aid within the meaning of article 87 of the ec treaty. the fact that regulation (ec) no 2204/2002 includes provisions on employment aid in favour of disabled workers does not mean that all state measures in favour of disabled workers are to be considered as state aid. as made clear in recital 6 of regulation (ec) no 2204/2002, some state measures in favour of disabled workers do not qualify as state aid, for instance because they are general in nature. such measures will continue not to be considered as state aid in the future. the purpose of the block exemption is to ensure that member states are not obliged to notify the commission of those state measures which do indeed constitute state aid under article 88 of the ec treaty, as long as the aid measure concerned fulfils a number of conditions as specified in the regulations.

in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. in the light of eu law, control of the external borders of the european union remains the responsibility of the member states, including poland. the current possibilities for providing assistance at european level for border checks at external borders and for the protection of these borders should unfortunately be considered insufficient. we must not forget this, because the proper management of the european union's external borders is aimed at combating trafficking in human beings and illegal immigration on the one hand, and at preventing threats to the internal security of the member states, public policy, public health and international relations on the other. such control is therefore not only in the interest of the member state in whose territory it is carried out, but is equally important for all member states which have abolished border controls at internal borders. the european agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders of the member states of the european union (frontex) has already been established by a council regulation. now we have to take it a step further. rapid intervention teams should be set up and deployed in the territory of the member state in need of such assistance, but not intended to provide long-term support. the agency should, however, be responsible for coordinating the composition, training and secondment of rapid border intervention teams. this approach will contribute to increasing solidarity and mutual assistance between member states.

striking. their heads of government first acknowledged their regional responsibility in the zimbabwe conflict at a special summit on 28 and 29 march 2007. president mbeki has been given a clear mandate to initiate a dialogue between the government and the opposition. he is expected to be flanked in his activities by his tanzanian counterpart, kikwete, who is currently the chairman of the sadc political, security and defence committee. the sadc secretary-general will present a report on the economic situation in zimbabwe. the sadc's main demands to mugabe are that the 2008 presidential election be held on schedule and that the repression of the opposition be stopped. the zanu-pf central committee decided on 30 march to hold the presidential election in march 2008 and to postpone the parliamentary elections originally scheduled for 2010 to the same date in 2008. mugabe was elected without internal debate as the top candidate. at the same time, changes were announced that would improve the starting position of mugabe and his party in the run-up to the elections. these include the increase in electoral districts and their redistribution, the appointment, not direct election, of senate members in correlation to the strength of the parliamentary faction, and the fact that in the event of a vacancy in the presidency, the new president is to be chosen by parliament rather than by new elections. these new regulations have yet to be implemented by constitutional amendment. the government has not stopped using force against individual opposition members. it stigmatises members of the tsvangirai wing of the opposition mdc party as terrorists and thus attempts to drive a wedge into the opposition, united for the first time since the march riots. however, the government has refrained from banning or dissolving large gatherings such as the prayer meeting in the country's second-largest city. the ban on assembly and demonstration has also been lifted, except in some areas of harare. as early as late 2006, the zanu-pf party congress showed that mugabe was no longer uncontroversial. mugabe has since developed a "bunker mentality" which has manifested itself in the formation of parallel organisations such as the "youth militia" which is outside the military and police hierarchy. their impressive, even depressing, presence in front of the central committee meeting building certainly had an influence on the decision-making of the politburo members in favor of appointing mugabe as a presidential candidate. despite mugabe's tactical victory in the march 30th central committee meeting, which earned him the nomination for the 2008 presidential nomination and weakened his critics within the party, there seems to be a sort of end-time mood in zimbabwe. the eu has therefore started to reflect on the post-mugabe period, alongside the discussion of current developments. we have been dealing extensively with zimbabwe in the last few days, both at the level of the eu-africa working group and the eu-africa directors. the foreign ministers' council discussed the crisis in zimbabwe on monday. the council in its conclusions welcomed the sadc initiative and expressed its readiness to support it if called upon . he underlined his view that only a broad constructive dialogue could form the basis for genuine reform and national reconciliation in zimbabwe. he also stressed that the eu would continue to implement humanitarian measures that directly benefit the population. the sadc has called on the eu to lift sanctions in its communiqué following the special summit in march. we shall not be able to do so in view of the present situation on the ground. our policy must remain credible. we will - the council decided on monday - in response to the unrest in march, extend the sanctions list to include the police officers who bear the main responsibility for the current crisis and human rights violations. there is agreement among eu partners that a solution to the crisis in zimbabwe can only be achieved with african help. our african partners have explicitly asked the eu for patience following their political reversal in march. however, we shall continue to monitor closely whether and to what extent the sadc policy pursued is taking shape. but we know that we cannot just watch. the eu will have to position itself in the foreseeable future on the sadc initiative in terms of content. we will continue to respond to the events in zimbabwe with the necessary vigour. the eu cannot and will not remain silent on human rights violations.
member of the commission. madam president, the commission is very concerned about the current deterioration of the political and socio-economic situation in zimbabwe. in particular, we condemn the recent acts of violent repression against the opposition. the commission has also fully supported the statements issued by the german presidency condemning the recent violence, arrests and mistreatment of detainees. the government of zimbabwe was also called upon to release those detainees and to respect fundamental rights. the crisis should be resolved through dialogue with all political forces. last monday, the general affairs council also issued conclusions to this effect. in this context, the commission continues to attach great importance to enhanced dialogue with zimbabwe’s regional peers. we fully acknowledge the major role they can play in promoting national reconciliation in this country. the commission therefore welcomed the extraordinary summit of heads of states of the southern african development community (sadc), which took place on 28 and 29 march 2007 in dar es salaam. the regional leaders decided to engage in the resolution of the zimbabwe crisis by appointing the south african president, thabo mbeki, as a mediator. it was agreed with all the european member states that a high-level message would be delivered to sadc on the subject. firstly, to recognise the major role the organisation can play in the resolution of the crisis and, secondly, to give sadc real breathing space in its mediation efforts. we feel, therefore, that nothing should be done to jeopardise the sadc initiative and that the eu should be seen to be ready to follow sadc efforts to resolve the zimbabwean crisis. furthermore, it was agreed to make an effort to properly inform the region and africa at large of the content of eu measures, or sanctions, regarding zimbabwe. they consist of a visa ban for the zimbabwean leadership and the freezing of their assets, in addition to an arms embargo. trade, economic and essential aid cooperation has not been affected by the eu measures. in this sense, the level of aid committed to zimbabwe in 2006 alone was around eur 193 million: eur 86 million by the commission and eur 107 million by member states. this kind of assistance, for the direct benefit of the zimbabwean population, is due to be continued.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. i have the honour to present to you the report of my own initiative from the committee on regional development on the contribution of future regional policy to the european union's innovation capacity. today, the community has two fundamental objectives in regional policy: to strengthen cohesion in all its dimensions and to promote and develop pro-innovation activities. it is not a trivial statement to say that basically everything that happens in the european union happens in some region, in some town, in some village. so it is not here, and more specifically, not just in brussels or strasbourg, that our future is decided. at present, about two thirds of community law is implemented at regional and local level. this report, which we have discussed very fruitfully in the committee on regional development, is addressed to the member states and the european commission, but above all to regional and local authorities. it is also addressed to other actors, in particular academic centres, research centres and small and medium-sized enterprises, which can be very effective flexible vehicles for innovation. regional policy cannot be reduced to the approval of projects and the better or worse management of the structural funds, but must be part of building the european union's innovation capacity. these capacities must be understood as complementary activities of a research-technological, legal-financial, economic-commercial, organisational-administrative, energy-environmental, educational, social, health-related and cultural nature, in other words, covering the whole range of activities. everywhere we go, we can do something new, something better. i would like to stress that each of these aspects has a regional dimension. this is to serve the real cohesion of the union, to be a testimony to the harmonized sustainable development and the community solidarity we have spoken of many times here. this is also intended to reduce the existing, and clearly disparate, development between the various regions of the union. we should also remember that a well-managed regional policy encourages innovation, which in turn leads to further development. so this is a very beneficial feedback loop. i do not want to repeat the report's assertions here. and i would like to take this opportunity to thank all of you who have helped shape it. i thank my colleagues here in brussels, strasbourg and poland. i thank all the members of the commission, and especially the coordinators, for the fruitful discussion and the amendments. i thank the representatives of the european commission, the committee of the regions and the presidency. it was very creative, as was mr andria's report (e.g. the supplement by alfonso andria?). it should be noted that of all the regions in the union, only 21 regions, i.e. less than 10%, have r & d expenditure above 3% of gdp. if we are to implement the lisbon strategy, then a more active contribution from the regional level is necessary. the other point i wanted to make is that we need to have universal and equal access to education at all levels, including university. this is the key to the future development of the community. yesterday, in this room, nobel prize winner timothy hunt lamented that in the ranking of the top 20 universities in the world, 15 are american, 1 is japanese, 3 are british and 1 is swiss. it's a signal of what we need to do as a community. the low-cost internet access, the financial tools, the rural areas, the innovation criteria of the regions also play a very important role. and the others are awake. we're debating this, but every day, 25,000 new citizens are born in china, 31,000 in india, and the population of europe is declining. our innovation must also include family issues. let's not waste time, money or energy, let's reach for solutions, they are not easy, but who said that only easy problems should be solved?
on behalf of the uen group. - madam president! - i have to go. i would like to draw attention to two points in this debate. first, the european charter for housing defines housing as a basic need and a fundamental social right underpinning the european social model. it is therefore good that the european regional development fund for the period 2007-2013 provides support for housing in the new member states, where the housing needs of the younger generation of citizens are particularly high. the difficult situation on the housing market in these countries is aggravated by the rapid increase in house prices of several tens of per cent per year due to the objective process of equalising property prices in the old and new member states. secondly, the impact of regional policy on innovation in the european union is limited by the limited resources allocated to this purpose by the union and other member states. the total union budget is just 1% of the community's gdp, of which less than 10% is spent on research and development. moreover, the average expenditure on this purpose in the union countries is less than 2%, whereas in the most developed countries of the world it is many times higher, so that the gap in this respect is widening rather than narrowing. to increase the level of spending to this end significantly, additional efforts by the union itself, additional resources from national budgets, but also financing of innovation from regional and local budgets and private sector spending are needed.

mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop this. ladies and gentlemen of the house! first of all, i would like to congratulate mrs pleguezuelos on her report, which tackles the important issue of the effectiveness of structural policies. the european union's cohesion policy takes advantage of structural policies and is a fixed, permanent component of the european union's policies, while its content and methods change. it is worth emphasising that the lisbon strategy is such a transitional, temporary policy. cohesion policy, on the other hand, is a permanent and permanent policy of the european union. cohesion policy is effective when it achieves its objectives and thus increases economic, social and territorial cohesion. however, this effectiveness depends on several factors. it is necessary to ensure the complementarity of the various policies of the european union, both community and national, coordinated at union level. secondly, cohesion policy should be adapted to the current development challenges of the european union, for example by reducing disparities between regions in terms of the development of the knowledge-based economy and the level of innovation. thirdly, cohesion policy requires the involvement of all types of public authorities in its implementation and therefore the way in which the author refers to government, regional and local authorities in many places in the report should be appreciated. multi-level governance is a necessary condition for an effective cohesion policy. the debate on the report coincides with the presentation of the fourth cohesion report by the european commission and provides a useful policy recommendation for analysing the data contained in the report and for drawing conclusions from the analyses contained therein.

member of the commission. mr president, we have heard some very well informed and very intelligent contributions to this debate. i appreciate them and thank those who have taken the trouble to speak. i think that the spirit, if not absolutely every letter, both of my own approach and of mr caspary’s report was captured by mr fjellner when he said that free trade spreads prosperity while protectionism spreads poverty. broadly speaking, i think that is correct but i would say that free trade is a necessary but insufficient condition to bring about economic development and poverty alleviation in some of the more needy countries of the world. i agree with those, including mr désir, who would like the commission to operate a principle of proportionate reciprocity as far as developing countries are concerned. i agree with that and my approach reflects the capacities of the developing country markets in question. the eu asks of trading partners only what their level of development allows but, as others have pointed out, the sorts of economies that are seeking free trade agreements with us – korea, the asean countries, india – could hardly be described as typical least-developed countries in the world. mr arif focused on the so-called singapore issues, as did mr désir himself. all i can say in this regard is that, if partner countries decide that they wish to discuss these issues bilaterally with the european union as a means of promoting their own development and creating economic opportunities for them, why should they not do so? i do not think it is for us in europe to tell developing countries and emerging economies that they should not be addressing issues like investment, competition and transparency in government procurement. one or two honourable members have alluded to trade defence. mr caspary did at the outset and mr guardans cambó has done so subsequently, as has mrs saïfi. there is no question in my mind of removing europe’s right of recourse to anti-dumping measures. trade defence instruments are a vital way of ensuring fair trade where goods have been produced in conditions of subsidy or where price distortion is taking place. of course that should not be confused with the ordinary low-cost advantages in trade for many developing countries. our purpose in using trade defence instruments is not to protect european business from fair low-cost competition. it is true that from time to time i sometimes encounter those seeking use of tdi because they are afraid of competition, not because they want to engage fairly in competition. but i think that a periodic review allows us to ensure that public confidence in these instruments is maintained and to make sure that, if necessary, these instruments can change in order to reflect a changing world. that is all we are doing. i should like to go back to one or two points that have been made. as regards the question of services liberalisation, i have quite a lot of sympathy with mr kamall’s point. yes, we will be looking at market opening in the services sector in our bilateral fta negotiations, but this will be a negotiation where our partners will maintain the right to regulate their services sectors and their right to decide whether or not to open public services sectors. that is for them to decide. it is not for us to impose. i am also glad that one or two honourable members have focused on the issue of labour conditions, social conditions and environmental conditions amongst our trading partners. i passionately believe that sustainable development, which touches on all those issues, is an overarching objective for trade policy as well. one trade and environment issue that we have pursued vigorously in the doha talks, but which some countries have opposed, is lowering tariffs on environmental goods. many environmental problems could be addressed by helping this trade. in future ftas we will also continue to include commitments to standards at the workplace. honourable members will know that we run into some opposition from our negotiating partners in respect of these conditions. they see them not as a way of levering up standards but as a way for those in the developed world to use new pretexts to keep their markets closed to the goods and services being exported from developing countries. so it important for us to keep a balance in these matters and certainly, as far as these issues are concerned, i strongly believe that we should be using the pressure that we have at our disposal by means of incentives, not sanctions. mr markov and mrs mann both touched on the issue of the role of the european parliament. i have always been interested in and committed to close cooperation with the european parliament in the context of the framework agreement that we have. wherever possible we extend our participation with the parliament on trade matters. that is why we have shared with parliament the negotiating directives for the ftas in an entirely transparent way. i would like just to touch on something that mr papastamkos said. in addition to his reference to our pursuit of zero taxes for an agreed list of environmental goods, i believe and i accept that we need to examine and find a way to deal with the free-rider issue in respect of climate-friendly policies and in connection with the kyoto protocol. in the long term this is going to become an increasingly important feature of the climate change debate. i think it is premature to think of a carbon tax. in my view, there are very many practical as well as legal difficulties in pursuing that specific idea. we must be careful that any climate-friendly policies and instruments that we might develop in the future do not become protectionist instruments. however, i entirely accept that the time has come for us to look carefully at these issues, because they are going to become increasingly relevant in the long term. i should like to thank all those honourable members who have spoken and contributed so well to this debate. i look forward to continuing and strong cooperation between myself and my services and this parliament.
