member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, david martin, for what i regard as a very rich report on aid for trade. i am very glad that he has referred to the millennium development goals, because they represent our guiding idea and targets. i agree with him that free trade, whilst a necessary condition for development, is not a magic wand, just as i agree with him that aid for trade, whilst a necessary component of any development strategy, is not a panacea. i believe that this report expresses a very strong commitment to the aid for trade agenda which i fully share. i have also read the very useful suggestions and guidance regarding the content of the eu joint aid for trade strategy, for which i am very grateful. furthermore, i welcome parliament’s engagement in this process. since 2005, the european parliament, the council and the commission have developed a clear common vision on the main principles of aid for trade. we all agree that trade can be an important catalyst for growth and poverty reduction in developing countries, but the successful integration of developing countries into the world trading system requires more than better market access and strengthening of international rules. in this respect the general affairs council conclusions of 14 and 15 may this year recall the crucial role of aid for trade. the challenge we are now facing is to put these principles into practice in the context of the eu aid for trade strategy on which the commission and member states are jointly working. this strategy should set out a roadmap to meet our financial pledges, give guidance to improve the effectiveness of our aid, provide a framework on monitoring and reporting of aid for trade, and address the capacity of the commission and member states to deliver aid for trade. the strategy will be ready in october of this year and will then be presented at the wto aid for trade review, so this parliament’s report is extremely timely. i would like to address some specific concerns raised in the report, and first of all the issue of the broadening of the scope of aid for trade in relation to the eu financial pledges. let me emphasise that the credibility of our pledges is of great importance and make it crystal clear that there will be no changes to the scope of our pledge. the eur 2 billion target remains related to the categories of trade policy and trade development. i attach great importance to the wider aid for trade agenda, which includes building productive capacities beyond trade development, infrastructure and adjustment aid. for these areas, which are very capital-intensive, we need clear political commitment to do more, but let me stress once again that these efforts will not be counted in relation to our financial pledges. regarding the lack of additional resources for edf funding to acp countries, we would be happy to do more, but the commission does not decide on the budget for the edf. eu member states do that. there are limited exceptions only and these are also approved by member states and dedicated to very specific purposes such as adjustment arising from the sugar reform. regarding the integrated framework, i am glad to confirm what i announced in hong kong. the commission is ready to commit eur 10 million over the first two years to the multilateral part of the enhanced integrated framework. in addition to this, the commission will complement the multilateral window with substantial bilateral and regional funding to implement activities identified through the integrated framework and prioritised by the respective partner governments. we will also provide human resources and capacity in the field to contribute to a better functioning of the integrated framework. the issue of adjustment aid is rightly highlighted in the report. however, i do not agree that the epa negotiations deserve a special mention in this context. adjustment aid is relevant in relation to all external trade shocks. they may result from trade negotiations but could also be a consequence of unilateral reform as in the case of sugar. in any outcome of the epa negotiations, the implementation of obligations of acp partners will be phased in over a very long period and this will facilitate adjustment and identify requirements that we need to help meet. finally, we noted your request to look into the imf’s trade integration mechanism as part of the eu aid for trade strategy. we think that this is more appropriately addressed in cooperation with other international donors, for example as part of the global aid for trade review at wto level. let me once again express my deep appreciation for this parliament’s political support for aid for trade, as well as our willingness to cooperate with the european parliament to make further progress, and i look forward to doing so.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: why aid for trade? because commerce has a serious mission to fulfill. a few points. good trade has brought people together for centuries without invading their identities, values, social and political life. europe needs equal partners among the big players, and especially the small players. trade must be governed by clear rules that take into account the interests of each party. 'fair and free trade' is a slogan worth supporting. fair trade cannot work without the right infrastructure, without agreements, for example, within the wto. without the appropriate manufacturer-customer protocols in place. it should not be forgotten that trade aid also means support for the vulnerable sectors themselves, such as sugar and soft fruit. in addition, cross-border exchanges between the union and neighbours such as ukraine should be encouraged. the global exchange scene is so diverse that there is a need to standardise and make these standards known to all citizens. the commission has therefore set up an aid programme that takes advantage of europe's historical experience, the wealth of goods, services and know-how on offer in europe, and has allocated funds for this purpose. small, but necessary. by analogy, good trade has the potential not only to raise living standards, particularly in the poor countries that this report is about, but also to contribute to a more peaceful resolution of world conflicts. mr. chairman, please! finally, i would like to refer to the anecdotal assessment that ryanair does more for a common europe than some european institutions, because it brings people together; i would say that fair and free trade does more for the integration and well-being of the people of the world, including poor countries, than dubious political decisions. the commissioner is committed to the fact that trade is the world's glue, so let europe be the promoter of aid for trade in this sense.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the house, in the european union, there is much talk of a sustainable multilateral trading system and of developing countries participating in and benefiting from trade. however, this concern has not gone hand in hand with the improvement in the situation of the least developed countries. on the contrary, their share of world trade has fallen by almost half over the last 40 years, from 1.9% to 1%. the displacement of retail trade and the transfer of income from less developed countries by strong large-scale trade networks is also clearly visible. these facts show that globalization and trade liberalization clearly serve to concentrate capital in the stronger countries and to increase poverty in the less developed countries. in recent years, we have seen a new approach to trade in the european union. it is manifested by a concern for the export of industrial goods at the expense of agricultural goods. this leads to a gradual loss of food security throughout the union, and particularly in the new member states. these facts make it necessary to introduce a new approach of the european union to international trade and to develop and implement national strategies for the development of trade.

the european union must, of course, have the right instruments in the form of institutions and policies to actively contribute to peace, stability and international security. but behind these tools there is always the political will of the member states, or the lack of it. europe is and will be as long as the political will of its leaders is there. the common foreign and security policy is also the political will of our leaders. so what are the challenges facing our leaders in terms of the cfsp and the sdg? firstly, i believe that whatever the final shape of the reform of the treaties, those proposals which are contained in the constitutional treaty and which directly or indirectly relate to the common foreign policy should be put on the road to reform. so give the european union a legal personality and get rid of its pillar structure. establish a new body, i.e. the post of minister for foreign affairs, and establish a european external action service. the general principle of unanimity should also be maintained in the field of foreign, security and defence policy, but the scope of qualified majority voting should also be extended. it is essential to introduce a solidarity clause in the event of a threat or terrorist act and to maintain the principle of mutual assistance in the event of armed aggression on the territory of any member state (principles formulated in article i-41 of the constitutional treaty). in addition, it is necessary to maintain structured cooperation in the field of missions while eliminating their exclusive character. the treaty should also include an extended list of tasks for st petersburg and finally establish a european defence agency. secondly, the effectiveness of the peacekeeping missions, both the current ones in bosnia and lebanon and the future one in kosovo, must be ensured. finally, a clause on energy solidarity should be introduced in the new treaty. it would be a good response to the threats to the energy security of the member states, which are increasingly affecting our citizens.

the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the situation in nigeria is of great importance for the stability of west africa and ultimately for the whole continent. the recent elections in nigeria were very disappointing. the council also expressed this in its statement of 27 april. there were numerous irregularities and violent incidents. up to 200 people were killed, many more were injured or intimidated. the council expects those responsible for these acts of violence to be held to account. fortunately, at least no religious or ethnic conflicts were detected in this election. there was an improved legal framework for these elections. substantial funds have been made available. all this had raised our expectations that the 2007 elections would be better than the 2003 elections. we are still waiting for the final report of the eu election observation mission, but some initial assessments suggest that the 2007 elections were even worse than the 2003 elections. the main problems were poor organisation, especially the late opening of polling stations, the lack of ballot papers and the fact that the elections were not secret. the fact that widespread irregularities were accompanied by substantial electoral fraud was even more serious. another serious problem in the elections was that detailed results were not published. in addition, the results were calculated in an unintelligible way. at this point, we should ask the nigerian authorities to publish the results and break down the numbers by polling stations. only in this way can the transparency of the electoral system be guaranteed. however, positive and encouraging for the council were the signs of increasing judicial independence during the election campaign. we hope that this trend will continue after the elections. the lively discussions in the private media before and after the elections were also encouraging. the council was impressed by the commitment of the nigerians themselves to this democratic process. the involvement of civil society organisations is and remains therefore of great importance. the council called on all political actors to use peaceful means and to behave responsibly by consistently applying the legal procedures in order not to disappoint the nigerian people. we hope that the independent national electoral commission and other bodies will quickly provide the evidence that the electoral courts need to complete their work as quickly as possible. the council also hopes that the nigerian authorities will be positive about the possibility of a repeat of the elections in cases where there is clear evidence of serious electoral fraud. but this is not the time to turn our backs on nigeria. on the contrary, i am. the stability and development of nigeria is of vital importance not only to the nigerian people but to africa as a whole. if the millennium development goals are not achieved in nigeria, then we cannot achieve them in africa at all. the future government of nigeria will face many challenges. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the government. the council will therefore continue to follow developments in nigeria closely.
member of the commission. madam president, as we have just heard, nigeria has recently held important elections that will determine the transfer of power from one civilian president to another. on the invitation of the nigerian authorities, the commission fielded a large independent election observation mission (eom), which performed well and cooperated closely with other international and domestic observer groups. i appointed mr van den berg – who had also observed the elections in 2003 – chief observer for those elections, and he will shortly give us his report. the mission concluded that the 2007 state and federal elections fell short of basic international and regional standards for democratic elections, pointing out that they were marred by poor organisation – as has already been cited, a lack of essential transparency and safeguards, widespread irregularities, significant evidence of fraud and disenfranchisement of voters. sadly, at least 200 deaths from election-related violence were also reported. other international observers – including those fielded by the economic community of west african states (ecowas) and the us national democratic institute, led by madeleine albright – were also very critical, as were domestic observation groups. the eu presidency expressed disappointment at these elections not having marked progress in relation to 2003, which has now been reiterated by our president, at the irregularities and at the high toll of victims. the reactions and the messages from the international community had been consistent in urging nigerians who have complaints about the process to use the legal provisions outlined in the constitution and in the electoral act, commending the independence shown by the judiciary and the engagement of civil society and praising the commitment of poll workers and voters. disappointment at this missed opportunity is widespread in the international community, as nigeria – one of the major powers in africa – could have set an example of successful consolidation of the democratic process, which would have had a tremendous positive impact on the african continent. this is even more regrettable as the elections were held in an improved atmosphere in which the freedoms of assembly and expression were at least broadly respected. the elections have highlighted the many problems and shortcomings of the nigerian democratic process, and the commission is aware that many challenges and misgivings need now to be addressed and overcome. in the short term, pressure should be placed on nigeria’s independent national electoral commission to publish a complete breakdown of the polling station results, which is a basic requirement of transparency, and the judiciary should also be encouraged to act swiftly and responsibly with the election petitions. if redress is not provided, this could have serious implications for the future. while the lessons learned will have to be taken into account in our future relations with nigeria, entrenching positions should be avoided. i think the political dialogue has to restart, but future relations will have to include a deeper engagement at federal, state and community level with a wider range of players in civil society and government. the topic of the elections must be a key feature of the political dialogue with nigeria, based on the 9 of the cotonou partnership agreement, the programming of the development cooperation to be financed by the 10th european development fund will also provide a crucial avenue for dialogue and the opportunity to take into account lessons learnt from the elections and the outcome of the discussions with the new government, civil society and other key players.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the aim of the document is to implement the lisbon strategy and to lay the foundations for a european innovation policy. the aim is to use the tools for implementing this policy in a way that improves the approach to research, the flow of knowledge to the economy and the implementation of innovative solutions in economic and social practice. the first question to ask is: what is innovation? the definition of this concept is important because innovation is the subject of large amounts of funding in regional development operational programmes. this term should be understood to mean any innovative solution to the problems encountered in the field of shaping the human environment, that is, the creation and use of its tangible and intangible products, including in the provision of services. the aim of innovation is therefore always to rationalise the production and use of products and the provision of services. this is related to the efficient use of energy and materials, as well as working time and the protection of both the workplace and the environment. so it's about doing things that lead to an increase in the quality of human life. it is, of course, necessary to exclude any artificial innovation concerning known products placed on the market under a new name. unfortunately, this is a common practice, often preceded by false advertising. the broad approach to innovation problems, which is what we are talking about, makes it possible, as defined above, to implement the innovative solutions known in one place in places where they have not been used before. in this case, the criteria for local innovation seem to be set by the local authorities with the help of experts. it's about getting the right funding for these things. the key drivers of innovation are: a well-functioning eu market for commercial products and services, taking into account all four freedoms; adequate innovation and education, but above all its structure, as graduates from studies with low innovation potential currently predominate; better practical use of the huge intellectual potential of research centres, especially in the new eu countries; better use of tax incentives, for example, to create an innovation fund, as well as loan guarantees, public procurement and public-private partnerships. innovation also stimulates synergies, including the creation of uniform community standards and norms. finally, the incentives for innovation are the appropriate intellectual property regulations. broadly speaking, innovation covers three groups of innovative solutions. the first is the rationalization of all types of activities, including administrative, educational, tourism, business and many others, which simplifies processes and reduces the time it takes to complete them, but does not bear the hallmark of invention. this kind of innovation requires a lot of practical knowledge. the second group of innovative solutions concerns innovation based on inventions which are patentable or form the basis of industrial or utility designs. this type of innovation requires a great deal of theoretical, practical knowledge, much of which is acquired, among other things, in patent offices. finally, the third group of solutions concerns innovative research on new strategic designs, systems and technologies carried out on a large scale in the framework of european or national research programmes. innovative basic research, and especially applied research, is producing, among other things, pioneering markets and new patents. the proper development of the second and third groups of these types of innovation requires a unified community patent and licensing strategy and the establishment of an innovation hub in the form of the european institute of technology. the current patent systems - there are as many in the eu as there are in the member states - are too expensive and the procedures take too long. the lack of a well-functioning, cheap and efficient european patent system is not conducive to innovation. the current patent policy of the european union countries is favourable to large corporations, which impose conditions of competition favourable to them by means of patent claims. this is not conducive to small and medium-sized enterprises, which could be the biggest innovators. in conclusion, i would like to say that innovation in economic and social life depends both on the proper functioning of purely market mechanisms and on eu and national regulatory action, including the way in which projects are supported from budgetary resources. our task is to create a european innovation area through comprehensive, appropriate education, financial and fiscal, research, patent and information policies. i would like to conclude by expressing my sincere thanks for the fruitful cooperation of my colleagues, the deputies of the rapporteur, mrs toia, and mr kubacki, mr hammerstein, mr ransdorf and mr janowski.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. on behalf of the uen group, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur. two weeks ago i presented a report on innovation in the context of regional policy. i am grateful to the author for including this aspect in his report. i believe that mr gierka's report can help to make the results of scientific work, patents, inventions and rationalising solutions more effective and practical in the broad sense of the economy. without it, we are doomed. it is not about innovation for its own sake, or artificial or false innovation. there is an urgent need to really tap into the work of the scientists, inventors and engineers who create real added value for europe and for our entire civilization. we need to look at where the brakes are on innovation, whether our bureaucracy is a particular obstacle. the union institutions, member state governments and regional authorities should play a stimulating role in these positive actions. the regions are often home to excellent universities, research centres and clusters. we have talked about the obvious role of small and mediumsized enterprises here. however, financial instruments, including taxation, and the proper use of the structural funds should not be forgotten. of course, innovation is particularly about building technology, especially today digital engineering, nanotechnology, materials engineering, biotechnology, medicine and so on. this is a huge opportunity for the european institute of technology and the proper use of the 7th framework programme.however, it should be stressed that innovative activities in education, management, administration, various services, agriculture, the local economy and so on are also necessary. in conclusion, i would say that true innovation always has a human face, so that both the creators and the users of the innovation are at the service of man.

the president of india, mr abdul kalam, in his wise address to this house on 25 april this year, stated, among other things, that to achieve lasting peaceful solutions, one must have 'justice at heart'. this message has been met with your warm approval and applause. the reorganisation of agricultural markets discussed today has many advantages: it aims to simplify legislation and reduce administrative costs, thus making life easier for farmers. it also has one fundamental flaw: it is not 'fair at heart', because it does not correct the unfair subsidisation of farmers in individual markets. this is particularly true for the poorer farmers in the new member states. the poor get less, the rich get more. this has nothing to do with the fundamental principle of the european union, which is the principle of solidarity. the rules of the common agricultural policy are still clearly being violated in many sectoral markets. repeated attempts to introduce fair financing for farmers in individual markets have proved unsuccessful. the figures showing clear discrimination were ignored. the current proposal of the european commission still has the shortcomings of the market organisations. it is artificial, unfair and not based on the real situation. a vote for simplification is a vote for perpetuating injustice and discrimination. i therefore appeal in particular to the representatives of the new member states: do not vote for this simplification, because despite its apparent advantages it discriminates against your farmers! at the same time, i would like to ask the representatives of the old member states: are you aware that financial discrimination against the new members is a threat to the future of the european union as a whole, because it perpetuates the division of the union into rich and poor, because it contradicts the idea of building a strong europe that is supposed to compete on the global market? i shall therefore vote against the commission's proposal and against the report. i also believe that simplification of legislation is necessary, but only if the individual markets are fairly organised. the european state! madam president! we are debating today the simplification of the common agricultural policy. the proposal is to establish a single common organisation of agricultural markets to replace the 21 sectoral regulations currently in force. it will be possible to repeal some 41 council regulations containing more than 600 articles and replace them with one regulation. of course, these measures should be welcomed if they improve eu legislation and make it more understandable to farmers and taxpayers, but this seems unrealistic. i'll give you an example: the paying agency in poland is accepting direct payment applications for the third time. this year, they simplified it so much that we had a delay in filing it because the farmers had a problem filling it out. this simplification is intended to be technical in nature and cannot therefore be transformed into another reform of the common agricultural policy. the position of abolishing intervention buying-in on the pigmeat market is therefore unacceptable. i would also be more cautious in delegating regulatory powers from the council to the commission, as this could result in a reduction in the influence of the member states on the decision-making processes concerning the functioning of the first pillar of the common agricultural policy. the question is also whether it makes sense to make all these changes when we are in the process of reforming the fruit and vegetable and wine markets. we also do not know what the health check will be in 2008, what the future of the common agricultural policy will be. i believe that the direct payments system in the eu27 in particular should be harmonised and simplified, and the rates of subsidies should be aligned, so that we can talk about a level playing field. the simplicity of saps makes it worthwhile to consider simplifying it for the eu15. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'common carrier' in the context of the single market.
madam president! first of all, i would like to congratulate mr niels busk on his report on the difficult subject of the establishment of a single and common organisation of agricultural markets. replacing the 21 common market organisations with one horizontal council regulation on a common market organisation will certainly contribute to simplifying and streamlining the legal structure of the first pillar of the cap and to greater transparency of agricultural legislation. however, we must not forget that the creation of a single common market organisation is a process of technical simplification and cannot include elements of political change. the work currently under way on a new regulation cannot be seen as a revision of the accepted principles of the cap and should not be a pretext for changing the policy decisions taken on agricultural policy. in this light, the commission's proposal to abolish intervention buying-in on the pigmeat market, which is so important in poland, for example, is therefore unjustified. i am also concerned about the european commission's proposal to set up a single management committee for the common organisation of agricultural markets. will one committee with a limited number of national experts function efficiently? would this not help to limit the influence of the member states in the administration of market instruments? how does the commission intend to ensure the full presentation of national expertise in the comitology process? would it not therefore be advisable to set up at least several management committees, including one for the meat, milk and plant products markets? and one last thing. as regards the extension of the commission's powers, i would like to stress that only in technical matters which do not have a substantial impact on the functioning of agricultural markets is it possible to transfer the council's competence to the european commission. this means that the power to determine the standard quality, the system of classification of carcasses on the market for beef and veal, pigmeat, as well as the power to determine the trading standards on the market for eggs, poultry and live plants should be vested in the council and not the european commission. moreover, all political issues should continue to be addressed together with the council and parliament.
on behalf of the pse group. - madam president! - i have to go. the european commission's planned changes to the current intervention system for cereals, which exclude maize from intervention, are intended to solve the problem of increasing stocks of maize each year. i agree with the commission's argument that the intervention mechanism needs to be reformed, but the planned changes could do more harm than good overnight. the reform of the cereals market should be evolutionary in nature and the measures to be taken should address the existing problem in a comprehensive manner. farmers should have sufficient time to prepare for the changes. instead of immediately excluding maize from intervention buying-in, the solution should include the maintenance of intervention buying-in until 2008 and then its gradual abolition or the phasing out of the intervention system by setting maximum limits for the intervention buying-in of maize for each member state according to the level of its current production as is currently the case for the rice market (this would increase the transparency of the system and facilitate market management); and the possible maintenance of intervention buying-in of maize for a transitional period of 2 years, subject to stricter controls to prevent excessive stocks of maize grain. these solutions would make it possible to abandon intervention on the maize market without causing too drastic a disturbance of the market. intervention is not only intervention buying-in, but also support for exports from the free market in the form of export refunds. in this context, it is also necessary to modify the current instruments to support the export of cereals from the free market so as to allow the export of cereals from countries with disadvantaged locations such as austria, the czech republic, slovakia, poland and hungary. the main market for cereals from the european union is the north african and middle eastern region, which means that exported cereals must be transported by sea over a longer distance than those exported from western or southern european ports. this has worked well, while increasing the efficiency of grain exports. it would be worthwhile to continue this mechanism in the following marketing year. i would like my speech to be seen not as an expression of solidarity with the great hungarian people (according to the famous polish and hungarian proverb "polish hungary two nephews, and to the sword and to the glass", although in this case it could be paraphrased as "polish hungary two nephews, and to the sword and to the grain", which in hungarian would be "lengyel, magyar két jóbarát együtt, harcol arat s gabonát"), but as a certain logic of the proper approach to the abolition of the intervention system for maize.

in writing. the report rightly emphasises the need for europe to have a broad innovation strategy to improve the competitiveness of its economy. the innovation strategy should be based on the creation of specialised knowledge regions, the reform of patent law and the introduction of tax incentives for companies investing in research and innovation. in order to facilitate the flow of knowledge at the level of research centre-business, the rapporteur notes the need to promote specialised knowledge regions within the member states, to increase the importance of cross-border cooperation and to intensify cooperation with experts from third countries. in the spirit of the report, i believe that the european institute of technology should create conditions that enable the linking of knowledge centres with business by focusing on innovation and helping to stimulate competition in innovative sectors of the economy. the report also highlights the need for reform of patent policy in europe. it is clear that robust and fair copyright protection and patent systems are key elements in building an innovative knowledge-based economy and society.
in writing. i vote in favour of the report by professor adam gierk entitled 'putting knowledge to work: an enhanced innovation strategy for europe'. there's a very deep divide in innovation in the world today. on the one hand, there are the 'innovation frontier' countries, where the vast majority of the science, research and development sector is concentrated, and on the other hand, the 'periphery' countries, which can only act as importers or diffusion countries of innovation. the world leaders in innovation are the usa, japan and the european union, and the competitive atmosphere between these economies is a stimulus for their innovation. however, the european union has recently experienced a 'paradox of innovation'. the economic performance of the community can be considered disappointing in view of the opportunities offered by the single european market. the project to transform the eu into the 'most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy' is a testament to the union's awareness of the need for fundamental reform of the socio-economic system, and a testament to the ambition and optimism that such change is possible. in his report, the rapporteur very aptly points to the main causes of this situation in the eu and above all emphasises the need to develop an effective innovation strategy for europe.

administrative red tape. the second is even more important in this respect, because of what many of you have said. it is a proposal for a directive on the admission of highly-skilled workers. this directive may, in certain cases, directly apply to third-country artists and grant them facilitated access to eu labour markets. we can go back 15 years or 5 years, but now is the time to move, and together we can do something.
member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to express my thanks to the rapporteur, mr chmielewski, and to both the committee on fisheries and the committee on the environment, public health and food safety for the report. the objective is to have the proposal agreed at the june council next week. during discussions held in the context of the council preparations, many changes have been introduced to the original proposal, some of which go in the direction of your suggested amendments. as you are well aware, both cod stocks in the baltics suffer from over-exploitation, with the eastern cod stock falling so far below safe biological limits that it may be in risk of collapse in the near future. at the same time, ices has indicated that misreporting of catches occurs in 35 to 45% of cases in the eastern baltic, which not only results in an additional unaccounted fishing impact on the stock but also affects the accuracy of scientific advice. the current situation not only harms the cod stocks in the baltic but is also threatening the fishing sector reliant on this resource. cod is one of the most important fish stocks for the industry in the baltic. it is therefore crucial, not only from an ecological but also from a social and economic perspective, to bring fishing into balance with resource availability as soon as possible, so that fishers can once more count on stable and high catches. the multiannual plan presented by the commission has been developed on the basis of past experience with managing cod fisheries in the baltic and on several consultations held with stakeholders, member states and scientists. it aims at rebuilding the stocks not only towards safe biological limits but even beyond, to levels that will provide the highest sustainable catches, thus providing stability in the long term for the fishing sector concerned, by reducing total allowable catches and fishing efforts step-by-step to the levels corresponding to this objective. turning now to the report, the recitals of the plan correspond to the measures that are later outlined in the actual provisions. i can therefore only accept amendments 1 and 5, which correspond to the provisions of the plan, such as the request to specify the status of the eastern cod stock in the first recital. amendment 4 is acceptable in principle. however, the split into western and eastern parts is determined by scientific evidence that there are two separate cod stocks in the baltic, and not by the ecological features of the two areas. the report proposes several amendments to the rules outlining the procedure for reducing total allowable catches and fishing effort to sustainable levels. amendments 8 to 11 would result in a mitigation of the reduction process and would limit its application. in view of the serious situation of the stock and the need to limit all types of fisheries catching significant amounts of cod, i cannot accept these amendments. i am, however, aware of the need to define a system that the industry can deal with. the commission has therefore changed its plan by combining the summer ban and the days absent from port. this will increase flexibility for the industry, and will thus particularly benefit small-scale fleets, for which a fixed and rigid system is more difficult to work with. moreover, an article on the european fisheries fund has been included in the plan to ensure financial compensation for the industry. changes to the effort system mean that several of the provisions on control and monitoring have also been changed. the margin of tolerance has been raised to 10%, except for cod, and the rules on discharging have been deleted, which should correspond to the provisions of amendments 14 and 16 of the report. concerning amendment 15, the rules on entry and exit from the area have been changed as well, meaning that the specified requirements apply only where the vessel is leaving the area in which it has been fishing. as misreporting is presently one of the key problems in the management of the baltic cod fishery, it is crucial to improve these rules to monitor comprehensively how much is taken from which cod stock, and when. for similar reasons, i cannot accept amendment 13, which limits the requirement for a log book to vessels with a special permit for cod fishing. the report proposes to reduce the valuation period from three to two years and to introduce a provision on the monitoring of the socio-economic impact of the plan in amendments 17 to 19. new cod recruits enter the fishery at the age of two to three years on average. if an evaluation began during the second year, it would be very difficult to detect any effects on the stock and, consequently, on the industry. the commission is, however, planning a project that will monitor not only the ecological but also the socio-economic impact of the plan as a first step towards the impact assessment to be made in the third year of the application of the plan. finally, i turn to the three amendments tabled by mr schlyter last week. they are not acceptable to the commission for the following reasons. the objective of the basic regulation for the common fisheries policy is to ensure sustainable management in ecological, social and economic terms. it is therefore the commission’s responsibility to strive for a balance between these three pillars, albeit based primarily on scientific advice regarding the stocks. i thus consider a gradual reduction of tacs and fishing efforts until target levels are met, as advised by ices, to be a good balance in this respect. ices also recommended using relative targets such as fishing mortality instead of fixed ones such as biomass, because they are less sensitive towards scientific uncertainty and the environmental variations affecting the stock. in the current situation whereby a high level of misreporting is interfering with management and scientific advice and in view of the possible upcoming revision of the biomass reference points for the eastern stock, the inclusion of biomass targets is not appropriate. however, as an expected outcome of the plan is the improvement of the basis of scientific information, the inclusion of biomass reference levels could be considered in the course of the revision of the cod recovery plan, which is envisaged to take place after the plan has been in force for three years.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the council regulation in question is an important legislative proposal, long overdue, which seeks to address the vital needs of fisheries in one of europe's most specific waters. for that, at least, the authors of the document deserve congratulations. they have undertaken the difficult task of devising a long-term recovery and fishing programme for baltic cod, a fish that is the lifeblood of many families. it is the most important fish in the baltic and therefore of great interest to fishermen. the opinion of the parliament and the subsequent council decisions are genuinely emotional in the baltic. the report, which was likely to produce satisfactory compromises in these circumstances, relied on verified data and took as a starting point scientific forecasts on cod stock development and fishing opportunities. the necessary intervention by the fisheries committee in the council's legislative proposal was due to the need to take account in the document of the inevitable socioeconomic consequences of the announced fishing restrictions - i am glad that the commissioner has spoken about this. the rapporteur's amendment, which obliges the european commission to monitor these effects and to propose to parliament the necessary remedies, was adopted. the amendment recommending a reduction from 10 to 8%, i am speaking for the committee on fisheries, of the limitations on the number of fishing days required by the regulation, and an increase from 100 to 300 kilograms of the so-called reported limit, was also accepted. the commission also adopted a proposal from the eu council of ministers to change the margin of error in fishing logbook records from 8% to 10%. the proposal to increase the minimum size of cod caught in the baltic to 40 centimetres was also supported. it is difficult to escape the impression that the corrective programme contained in the document was substantially influenced by the belief that the fishing capacity of the baltic cod fleet is at the present stage far too high in relation to the available fishing quotas. however, there is still no proposal at eu level or at member state level for a systemic solution to this problem. there is a growing consensus that automatic decisions on scrapping the fleet should be avoided. instead, solutions should be sought to maintain a certain fishing capacity until the stock is restored. we must have something to fish for. i think that sooner or later the question of the length of the closed summer periods will be included in the discussion of the plan for the recovery of cod, as the commissioner has also said today. it should be noted that member states seeking to further reduce fishing effort by introducing additional cod days tend to prefer the so-called days at sea rather than the closed periods as in the past. the scientific consultations accompanying the general discussion of the council regulation indicate the need for a revision of the biological benchmark assessments that have been used so far, and i am also glad that the commissioner has mentioned this today. in addition, none of the baltic states is in principle opposed to the introduction of fishing mortality as a means of defining the objectives for the implementation of the multiannual plan for the recovery of baltic cod - i recall article 4 of the plan. it is necessary to have a thorough discussion on the biomass reference point level which is adapted to the actual state of the stock and the overall situation of the baltic sea ecosystem at the present time. this will be in line with the community's commitment to implement an ecosystem approach to fisheries management, recalling point 5 of the preamble. the current limit points, i stress, were adopted in 1998 on the basis of data from the 1970s and 1980s. they cannot therefore be adequate to the current herd dynamics. finally, it should be noted that the intention of the earlier council regulation 2371/2002, cited in the document under examination, was to exercise caution when making fundamental changes to the fisheries policy, caution relating both to the management of the stock and to the assessment of the socioeconomic effects of those changes. this principle should continue to apply after the accession of the new baltic four to the european union.
member of the commission. mr president, i would firstly like to thank you for the number of points that have been raised. i think it is clear that we share a common objective, that of ensuring the long-term sustainability of cod stocks in the baltic and thus the livelihood of the fishers in the region. while we may differ on the means of achieving this objective, i have no doubt that our aim is the same. on the specific points raised, i would like to make the following points. firstly, we must propose schemes for effort limitations and take into account the effort exerted by small-scale fleets since their catches represent around 50% of total catches. we are, however, ready to consider flexible mechanisms in order to enable them to apply the plan without it being too much of a burden. i would like to stress that the eastern cod stock has been declining continuously over the last decades, as has the average catch size. the serious situation of this stock is therefore self-evident and, while it is crucial to take account of the socio-economic perspective, it is primarily the ecological status which requires recovery, that is of paramount importance. in this regard, an annual reduction of 10% has been identified as the minimum in order to be able to detect changes in the development of the stock status or the sector deriving from the plan. a decrease of the annual reduction would also confront the sector with a longer reduction period and therefore delay the benefit of bigger and more stable catches and would make it unlikely that the msy levels can be reached before 2015, as is required under the johannesburg commitment. finally, it is important to underline that control is the key issue, particularly in this fishery. we hope to reach a solid and workable solution to this issue in the council next week.

member of the commission. mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur and the members for this very important task. this is a citizen-led policy, because neither the economy nor the market can bring broadband to the citizens in the regions. we all know that broadband is an accelerator of development and a reducer of inequalities, provided that citizens have access to it. so we have to deal with this access problem. i say 'we' because it is clear that the commissioner responsible for this matter cannot deal with it alone. that is why we have joined forces within the commission. so mrs kroes has started to work on this dossier - and i take this opportunity to thank her - a dossier in which she is deeply involved, and it must be said that state aid is an essential part of it. but there is also the commissioner responsible for rural development, the commissioner responsible for regional development and the commissioner responsible for consumers. a real pooling of responsibilities has therefore been achieved within the commission to solve the problems. i believe that mrs kroes has already told you that in the case of state aid, she has taken decisions to ensure that this aid is granted on very clear and very precise terms, at a time when the market itself is not enough to solve the problems. as regards the universal service, a broad discussion will be very useful. is it really necessary to extend the universal service, which does not include broadband today, or is it not necessary? i have already heard very different views in the debates this evening, and we will have to clarify them. that is why, with the green paper which i intend to present at the beginning of 2008, we are going to launch a broad debate which will enable us to see how to legislate or not to legislate in the future. as regards quite specific elements, it is clear that the commission will not only make speeches or organise conferences, such as the conference on bridging the digital divide in rural areas some weeks ago, but will also take specific action. for example, we will launch a website before the end of this year to act as a central information platform publishing calls for tender and providing a one-stop-shop for exchange of best practice. we hope that this website will become a virtual meeting point between suppliers and local governments. the second action concerns the new programming period of the structural funds and it includes the initiative 'regions for economic change', which aims to help member states implement the new lisbon strategy through action aimed at economic modernisation. this initiative includes two thematic networks on ict, broadband and e-government. finally, there will be the european transnational networks initiative that will help authorities planning transport and energy infrastructure and make them take account of the telecom needs as well, because deploying dacs and dac fibre alongside this infrastructure may reduce future telecom costs by 80%, so it will be very important to foresee the exploitation of synergies when making this kind of investment. having said that, i am also very aware of the fact that technologies such as wimax or satellites will be an alternative to fibre and dacs, for example. it has been asked whether we can provide more precise guidance regarding the use of structural funds, in particular where a partial supply of such a service already exists. since 2003, there have been guidelines for the use of structural funds in the electronic communications, but 2003 is a very long time ago in a field where technology is very fast-moving. that is why, over the past two years, the commission has developed the consistent decision practice of applying state aid rules to broadband support measures. most of the measures assessed contain structural fund co-financing. we have already issued 26 decisions in this area and those further clarify under which conditions public funds for broadband can be granted. having said that, i would also like to say that these eu funds are not allocated to private enterprises: they are allocated to public authorities and it is those public authorities, for example the regional authorities, who define their operational programmes. the commission does not supervise those projects except for the large projects over eur 50 million. those then undergo examination by dg regio, dg comm and/or dg infso. another point which has been made is the question of our citizens who suffer from some form of disability during their lifetime. now these may be disabled people, but we will also have an aging population. we have calculated that about 50% of our citizens will be disabled at least once during their lifetime. therefore, at the end of last month we issued a communication on ageing well in the information society. here we focus on making all ict services accessible to citizens and to help most of all those with special needs. i believe that this will go beyond the regional issues and the digital divide and will be one of the problems we will have to solve in the months and years to come. i would really like parliament to come forward on this issue, which will also be an important topic for discussion with our citizens, above all in the perspective of the european elections to come. i would like to make one last point. all this is wonderful, but we need spectrum and that is why we are working on having spectrum available for all these services which will be needed by one technology or another in our rural areas for our aging society. i am, of course, referring to health, but also to the issues of education and e-government, which are crucial elements. as for e-government, we will be holding a big ministerial conference, together with stakeholders, in september and will discuss how to make better use of the services in order to reach the population, important above all for the aging population and for people who live far from urban centres. secondly, the commission is working on making spectrum available for example for the 2.6 mhz band. i'm really counting on the positive effect of the digital dividend when we switch from analogue to digital, where we should be looking at the spectrum below 1 mb. this is very interesting indeed for the new services which we will need in order to have broadband for all. thank you, rapporteur, for the important work which has been done. this is only the beginning of the work we have to do together in order to make europe a place of balance between all citizens allowing them to access the new technology without a digital divide but, rather, with a digital dividend for our society.

be credible if states entrust the implementation of union law to appropriately empowered, competent and accountable institutions, which will be assessed for their effectiveness. the three factors implement the acquis communautaire, involves allocating the appropriate resources and staff. this is the aspect which the commission is putting the greatest emphasis on at present. but the third one, which is preparedness, is the most important one, in my opinion.

member of the commission. mr president, four years ago the commission announced its intention to develop a european security and defence policy. since then, we have been striving to establish a more open and fair european defence market through a number of initiatives. the new procurement directive for defence equipment is a crucial element of this overall strategy and is one of the commission’s strategic priorities for this year. at present, the vast majority of defence equipment tenders are conducted outside community rules. member states rely upon the derogation from the treaty under article 296. in the commission’s view, this derogation should be limited to the exceptional cases. we gave some guidance on the matter last december. nevertheless, the derogation is still the rule more than the exception. most defence procurement has therefore remained outside of the internal market principles. this means that all 27 member states procure defence equipment in accordance with their own national regulations, often resulting in non-transparent and sometimes discriminatory practices. we recognise that current public procurement rules are really suited to the particular needs of the defence procurement. but we believe we can achieve important economic gains if we open up national defence markets, which represent 0.8% of the european union’s gdp and one quarter of public procurement at state level. member states and industry widely acknowledge these advantages. fair and transparent conditions would allow companies, especially smes, to tender more easily in other member states and thus widen their access to business opportunities in a much larger home market. longer production runs would allow economies of scale. this in turn would help to reduce costs and lead to lower prices. the final beneficiary of that would be the taxpayer. our proposal would adapt certain community procurement rules to the specific nature of defence and give awarding authorities greater flexibility for sensitive procurement procedures. this will also make it easier for member states to use the derogation under article 296 of the treaty only in exceptional cases. as is the case under the other procurement directives, member states will continue exchanging views on defence procurement issues via the advisory committee on public procurement, once the directive has been implemented. i wish to emphasise that the new directive will implement the code of conduct of the european defence agency. the code of conduct applies only to contracts which are exempted from the community rules on the basis of article 296, while the future directive will apply to contracts which are not exempted from community rules. together the code of conduct and the new directive will enhance transparency and fair competion on defence partners in the european union. i am pleased to indicate that work on the proposal for a defence directive is well advanced. my services are member of the commission. mr president, i would like to express my thanks for this question and to inform members that the commission is well aware of the situation. frost struck fruit producers not does not foresee any direct assistance to producers adversely affected by climatic conditions or natural disasters. the cmo provides eu assistance to producer organisations and producer groups in relation to their operational programmes and in recognition of the plans that, to some extent, can cover losses. in the proposal for the reform of the common market organisation, the commission proposed to widen the scope of the crisis management tools and to enable the producer organisations to get eu co-financing to cover costs of harvest insurance and, later, to establish mutual funds. as regards the possibility of granting state aid, member states may, under certain conditions, use the provisions of regulation (ec) no 1857/2006 to exempt from notification an aid scheme earmarked for the compensation of losses due to frost. in case the envisaged aid scheme does not fully comply with the provisions of the regulation, member states may still notify it under the community guidelines for state aid in the agriculture and forestry sector, 2007-2013. i would also like to add that member states may also use the de minimis mechanism. in that case, the aid would be limited to eur 3 000 per beneficiary in three years, within the framework of the maximum amount laid down for each member state in the annex to the regulation. under the rural development legislation, member states have two possibilities to support producers who suffer from the consequences of natural disasters. firstly, member states may implement specific measures to restore agricultural production potential damaged by natural disasters, and they may also introduce appropriate preventive actions. however, the present draft proposal of the polish rural development programme for the period 2007-2013 does not foresee the inclusion of this measure in the programme. the commission is open to discussing this possibility with the polish authorities, should they wish to do so. another possibility of rural development support is provided under the force majeure rule of the rural development policy. in case a natural disaster seriously affects the land and the holding, and the farmer cannot respect the relevant commitments he has made under a rural development scheme, member states may recognise a case of force majeure. this means the farmers who benefit from rural development support will not have to pay back the aid received. one of the most relevant measures under force majeure is agri-environment. if, during a specific year, the beneficiary cannot respect the commitments due to a natural disaster, he will not be paid or partially not be paid in that year. however, he does not have to reimburse the payments he has received during the rest of the period of the contract. the member state is invited to discuss the different aspects of this case with the commission services. as regards the application of force majeure, it is important that the beneficiary notifies the case in writing to the competent authority, together with relevant evidence, within 10 working days from the day on which the beneficiary is in a position to do so.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. almost every year, in different regions of europe, we are confronted with a variety of natural disasters. we hear about droughts, heavy rains leading to floods, or strong winds. unfortunately, we've had a few frosts this year. these frosts, which occurred in the northern, central and eastern parts of europe in april and may, when the ground temperature dropped to as low as -10 degrees celsius, caused enormous damage to agriculture. early vegetables, apple trees, pears, cherries, plums, and soft fruits were among the crops affected. in some regions of poland, the losses are so high that this will have a significant impact on the financial situation of many farms. until now, polish farmers and fruit growers have rarely insured their produce because it is very expensive and often simply beyond their means. but the cold wave has not only affected my country, but also fruit growers and farmers, although to a lesser extent, in germany, the netherlands, the czech republic, slovakia, austria, hungary and even northern romania. i'm not going to let you do this. we need systemic action to provide not only financial support to affected fruit growers, farmers and processors, but above all solutions to prevent or mitigate the effects of natural disasters, which are becoming more frequent as a result of climate change.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. first of all, i would like to express my deep satisfaction that the euro area will be joined by two new countries on 1 january 2008: cyprus and malta. both countries have fulfilled the convergence criteria required by the treaty. i would like to extend my warmest congratulations to our cypriot and maltese colleagues. the enlargement of the euro area is an important process that deepens the integration of the member states of the european union. this process has a positive impact both on the candidate countries and on the euro area economy itself. countries preparing to join the euro area are developing at a much faster rate than euro area countries and are in a better macroeconomic situation, especially in terms of public debt and budget deficits. the accession of these new countries to the eurozone strengthens the whole area and the single currency. at the same time, i would like to express my dissatisfaction with the fact that parliament has to work under enormous time pressure when considering the accession of new countries to the euro area. the current tight work schedule does not allow parliament to prepare a sound opinion. the resolution we are - i hope - adopting today is therefore intended to launch the debate on an interinstitutional agreement which will allow the efficient and effective analysis of the convergence reports in the future. i am pleased that president barroso and commissioner almunia have just declared on behalf of the commission an open and constructive approach in this respect. i hope that the council of the european union will also take a constructive approach, mr gloser, and that we will be able to work out a smooth mechanism to allow future enlargements of the euro area to proceed smoothly. in the debate on the enlargement of the euro area, it should be stressed that some of the existing maastricht convergence criteria are not adapted to the current situation. this is particularly the case with the inflation criterion. first, it does not seem appropriate to base the criteria for joining the euro area on the average inflation rate in non-euro area countries. secondly, the current criterion does not take into account the fact that rapid economic growth in the new member states naturally translates into higher inflation, which is by no means a sign of economic weakness, but rather reflects the process of the new member states catching up with the developed economies of the old union. thirdly, i would point out that the definition of price stability used by the commission and the european central bank in their convergence reports differs from the definition of price stability used by the european central bank in its monetary policy. however, the treaty contains only one term, price stability, and no two different interpretations of that term can be used. the inflation criterion in its current form means that some of the new member states may not be able to join the euro area for many years. this creates a permanent division into two categories of member states: euro area countries and non-euro area countries. such a situation threatens the cohesion of the union and is contrary to the spirit of the treaty. the convergence criteria designed 16 years ago, under very different conditions, should be adapted to the new situation. i call for a serious debate on this.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. this report was originally intended to be a review of the commission's 2005 strategy communication and the strategy itself prepared by the council in the same year. but in the course of the work, it became clear that the work on the external dimension of the area of security, freedom and justice had made great progress, and had gained new impetus. they have brought new documents, new decisions and new actions, and our situation today is very different from that of a year and a half ago. i therefore decided to look ahead and not backwards, and this is the view adopted by both committees: the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs and the committee on foreign affairs, which worked on this report in enhanced cooperation. it should therefore not be surprising that this report is really a set of recommendations to the commission and the council. this report is based on two assumptions. first, that in the modern world, the external and internal aspects of security are intertwined, overlapping, and in fact, inextricably linked. secondly, that in our legal systems and political practice, it is necessary to maintain a balance between civil liberties on the one hand, and the security of our citizens on the other. this means that if we want to ensure both the security and the freedom of our citizens, we must promote both values outside the european union, but always in a certain balance. our foreign policy must therefore take account of these very assumptions and adapt its instruments to them: common positions, joint actions, bilateral or multilateral agreements. in other words, we should include both anti-terrorism and human rights clauses in agreements with third countries, for example. and in its ongoing cooperation with these countries, the european union should promote both respect for human rights and the common fight against international terrorism. we are also aware here in parliament of the limitations and barriers which currently exist and which reduce the effectiveness of the european union in this area. they are partly due to our complex and unclear institutional structure, but also partly to a lack of will to deepen european integration. within each pillar, decisions on cooperation and external agreements are taken according to a different procedure. and the long-awaited integration of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters into the community is still waiting for better times. these times must come as soon as possible. we expect the next european union summit to lead to an intergovernmental conference, such as the one that will present a draft new treaty by the end of this year, and that in this treaty the union will have legal personality, the existing pillar structure will be abolished, the number of categories of legal acts will be reduced and decision-making procedures will be simplified and standardised. but before that happens, before the treaty enters into force, because it can only come into force in 2009, this report calls for the application of a transitional clause, the passerelle, in accordance with article 42 of the treaty on european union, in relation to police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters and immigration policy in the field of legal immigration and the integration of foreigners. given the immigration pressure on our southern border and the threat of organized crime on our eastern border, it would be a very serious policy error not to do so. and speaking of borders, i would like to draw the commissioner franco frattini, for the good and fruitful cooperation.

also makes a lot of demands. it can be used for good or, unfortunately, for evil, as have many other tools that man has had in his civilization. the use of digital technology for electronic commerce, which involves the purchase of a wide range of goods and services, should also be seen in this context. the legal and technical solutions used should meet a number of criteria. that's what the report says. i would like to raise a few points in this context. first, access to the online shopping market should be much more widespread. hence the repeated issue of promoting broadband internet. currently, only about 25% of households in the european union have access to broadband, which means a good quality connection. secondly, the use of this form of purchase must be secure, both in terms of the transaction itself and in terms of obtaining an appropriate guarantee for the goods and services purchased irrespective of borders. thirdly, the frequent anonymity of transactions cannot in any way facilitate criminal activities such as piracy of copyrighted films or music. it is therefore necessary to clarify the term 'use for own use'. fourthly, activities such as the purchase of pedophilic material, pornography, the distribution of prostitution, etc. via the internet require particular police and prosecutorial activity. it's a slap on the wrist. fifth, payment made over the internet must be made in such a way that both parties to the transaction are fully secure. sixth, the advertising of goods or services which can be purchased by electronic means should enable the potential buyer to verify the information received. seventh, the security of digital banking transactions must be radically improved. eighth, new possibilities, especially in remote areas, of digital delivery of some medical services, diagnostics, remote monitoring are very important. ninth, another important topic in this area is distance learning. ten, let us remember that many of the benefits of consumer use of digital platforms are for people with disabilities. in conclusion, i would like to stress that without good quality, fairness, transparency and flexibility, we will not build a robust, competitive digital services market.

member of the commission. madam president, we have good reason to follow closely the recent developments in cuba, because after 47 years of ruling cuba fidel castro transferred power to his brother, raúl, who has been running the island in a relatively calm and organised fashion. it is too early to say whether fidel will fully recuperate from his illness, but nearly all observers agree that he will never be able to assume day-to-day management again. cuba, for the first time since the revolution of 1959, has to face the prospect of a country no longer fully run by fidel castro. this is definitely a new situation, which we must take into account. the question is: how can, and how should, the european union react to this new development? the council of the european union gave its first answer three days ago. in its conclusions on cuba of 18 june, the eu renewed its offer of an open and comprehensive dialogue with the cuban authorities and invited a cuban delegation to brussels to sound out the feasibility of such an exercise. this open-door approach is consistent with the eu’s overall policy of constructive engagement towards cuba. since 1996, when the european union adopted its position on cuba, experience has proved that only a policy of engagement and cooperation, not one of sanctions, has the potential to promote peaceful change in cuba towards democracy, respect for human rights, the rule of law, sustainable economic recovery and improvement in the living conditions of the cuban people, as stipulated in the eu’s common position of 1996. only the establishment of an open, comprehensive and result-orientated dialogue with the cuban authorities will enable us to make the best use of the variety of instruments the eu and its member states have at their disposal to further cooperation in the fields of political relations, human rights, investment and trade, development work, scientific research, educational exchanges and culture. the european union is a profoundly value-based entity that makes respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms a key policy priority in its external actions. it is deeply convinced that this commitment towards open dialogue must also involve wider cuban civil society. extending a hand to the cuban government to enter into a long-term partnership with the european union only makes sense if, at the same time, the european union does all it can to maintain and step up its dialogue with those involved in cuban civil society, including human rights defenders and peaceful political activists. as long as cuba denies its citizens internationally-recognised basic civil political and economic rights, the european union will not stop lobbying for democracy and respect for the rule of law and fundamental freedoms. it should not stop expressing its full solidarity with and support to those peacefully committed to making these universal values a reality in cuba. this is the true meaning of the ‘two-track approach’: saying ‘yes’ to extending a hand to the cuban authorities for dialogue and cooperation while explicitly expressing critical remarks and concerns, and ‘yes’ to defending the right of cuban citizens to decide freely about their future. it is the commission’s firm conviction that the council conclusions of 18 june are a welcome and necessary first step in this direction.
