member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the members for a very interesting debate. as i anticipated, on some issues we do not completely agree, but i am sure that with discussions and some goodwill on both sides we will be able to find solutions. to begin with, the priority for all of us, the main consideration, is the protection of the consumer, there is no question about that, and i am sure you do not doubt my willingness to promote the interest of the consumer in this respect, but at the same time we have to remain proportional, we have to be practical and we have to be able to achieve this target with the smallest possible administrative burden. i would like to refer to some of the issues, though i do not want to take up too much time. firstly, on the issue of codecision and comitology, maybe i should remind you that the reason we, the two institutions, agreed on the new principle of comitology with scrutiny was precisely to find a procedure through which we could have a practical, simple, speedy way of taking decisions on technical and scientific issues by giving a stronger say to the european parliament and having more transparency for the european parliament to be able to express its views. by the way, this has not been used yet, we have just started with that. my legislation on health claims was the first to adopt this, so referring to the old comitology procedure is not relevant to what we are discussing now because now we are discussing the new one, which achieves the targets of transparency and of involvement of the european parliament but at the same time allows a speedy and practical way of deciding on technical and scientific questions. imagine having to go through the whole legislative proposal every time you have to decide on an enzyme, on an additive, on a calorie, when at the end of the day it will all be based on the views of the european food safety authority that we have jointly, with legislation from parliament, created exactly for this purpose. i would ask parliament, or the sides of parliament which are keen on introducing codecision in this respect, to reconsider, because in the end we will not achieve any of the intended targets we have set and it will eventually, due to the lengthy procedures, work against the interests of consumers as well. on the issue of the legal basis, i agree with mrs doyle. you know our position and i believe that we should have a single legal base. i believe that this can cover all the other considerations, because the other considerations are reflected in the legislation itself. on the issue of allergenicity, i agree that this should be one of the legitimate factors to consider when authorising food additives, so it will be a factor to be taken into account. labelling, too, is a very important aspect and will help the consumers get information, but we could not accept a total restriction on those additives which may be allergenic as the consumers affected by those can be protected through the labelling legislation. on the double authorisation procedures with the gmos i agree that we have to have a practical and good administrative practice. therefore, we could accept the proposed clarification but with some rewording to make the text compatible with regulation (ec) no 1829/2003. on the issue of herbs and spices, i agree they are natural, but, at the same time, it does not mean that they do not contain certain substances naturally which can still pose health problems. that is why it is useful and important to also include those on the list and have the maximum levels. we had a situation recently in at least one member state where we had to consider the possibility of reintroducing maximum levels. therefore, just because something is natural does not necessarily, and by definition, mean that it does not also contain some substances that when consumed in excessive amounts can be harmful. on the question of nine months for the commission, six months for efsa, nine months is the maximum time proposed, but that does not mean that it will take nine months. however, at the same time, based on the opinion of efsa, there is a procedure for the commission to consult with the stakeholders and the member states to see how they can deal with the technological needs, the benefits to consumers and to ensure that consumers are not misled. there are many other relevant factors. as you know, consultation processes in the european union need some time. we have to be able to exhaust those processes. that is why we would like to have adequate time, but that does not necessarily mean that this time will be exhausted. on the issue of the benefits to the consumer, we could accept that these be included in a recital – this would reinforce an important principle – but not in a restrictive way in the legislation. i will not go into details. when we get our position we will be able to see the reason why we can accept part of it. on the issue of how the legislation on pesticides complements this legislation and vice versa, we believe that one complements the other. therefore, when a product is not covered under plant protection legislation it will be covered by this one. it is important for clarity to maintain a clear line between these two areas of legislation. i was specifically interested to see whether there was a possibility of creating a gap, and that is not possible. it is clear that one or the other pieces of legislation will assess the safety of the product, depending at what stage it is being used, and taking into account some technical aspects of it. on the issue of ‘natural’ and the question of 90% or 95%, it is important that when we refer to the source we have the highest percentage possible of that source. at the same time, the rest has to come from a natural source. on the other hand, if something is to be called ‘natural’ and not by reference to a specific source, then it has to be 100% natural. the main target for all this is to ensure that consumers are not being misled. at the end of the day, the most important aspect of the proposals is to assess safety, make sure that there is no risk to the health of consumers and provide information so that consumers can make an informed choice. it will be up to them to decide whether they want to buy a processed product or something natural and fresh. it is our basic policy to promote the consumption of fresh foods, but we cannot exclude the other products from the market. therefore we have to give consumers a choice and then they can exercise it according to their needs.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. i'm not going to let you do this. today's debate is the culmination of several months of debate in the european parliament on modernising labour law to meet the challenges of the 21st century. it was a very heated debate, sometimes turbulent, but nothing strange about it, because it was about an issue that affects almost every european, regardless of age, profession or place of residence. the intense discussion was not confined to this house. the publication of the green paper triggered a wide public debate throughout the european union involving numerous trade unions, employers' organisations, economic and labour organisations and many non-governmental initiatives in both the old and new member states. after these few months, i have the impression that most of the participants in the debate agreed that changes in labour law seem necessary in the face of the challenges of the present century. what are the challenges that we've been thinking about and talking about? the four main ones are: first, the positive and negative consequences for european economies of increasing globalisation. secondly, the rapid development of the services sector, which is creating more and more jobs throughout the european union and in the new and old member states, but with a very different character than the jobs created by industry. the third challenge is the rapid changes in technology, especially modern communication techniques, which are having a significant impact on the way work is done today. finally, a very important challenge is demographic change, which is already seriously changing the situation in european labour markets and will have an even more radical impact in the near future. while there was broad agreement on the need for change, the direction of change was no longer clear. some meps have advocated more flexibility in european regulations, arguing that this is a way to increase employment and reduce unemployment. others, on the contrary, called for the protection of labour law to be strengthened. some meps called for greater harmonisation of national legal systems, arguing that this was required by the progressive process of creating a single european market. others, on the other hand, strongly defended the principle of subsidiarity in this area, pointing to the different traditions and models in the member states and stressing that this diversity is a value, since it allows the best solutions to be found through practical exchange of experience rather than new, usually rigid community legal regulations. the draft report i prepared, as a draft of the european parliament's position, was in favour of greater flexibility and against harmonisation. it also included proposals for legislation which welcomed the impact of so-called non-standard forms of employment in creating new jobs in the european union and called on member states, inter alia, to apply active labour market policy methods and to promote adaptability in order to protect people rather than specific, existing jobs. in the preliminary draft report, i also pointed out the need to improve eu and national regulations in order to relieve businesses and citizens of unnecessary costs and burdens of red tape. i also pointed out that too restrictive labour laws can discourage employers from hiring new workers even in times of economic growth. i also stressed the crucial role of education in improving the chances of workers and the unemployed to find new jobs. in this context, i proposed to call on the european commission, member state governments and employers to invest more in lifelong learning and to improve the quality of education for young people, especially in relation to the needs of local and regional labour markets. finally, i stressed the importance of mobility for improving the european labour market. i therefore proposed to call on the member states to lift the restrictions on access to their labour markets imposed on nationals of other eu countries. the first draft report provoked a very lively reaction from colleagues in the parliament. the heated debate and the 490 proposed amendments to the original text were the subject of further discussion and negotiation with all political groups. i would like to thank my colleagues from the party of european socialists, and in particular mr christensen and his advisers, for their contribution to these negotiations. the outcome of the negotiations was voted on at the extraordinary meeting of the committee on employment and social affairs on 18 june in strasbourg. i must admit that the outcome of this vote was not entirely satisfactory to me. i have the impression that we have lost sight of a very important message which i proposed in the original draft and which i believe has not been substantially challenged in subsequent debates, namely that all reforms of the labour market, including the reform of labour law itself, should be geared to creating new jobs in europe in order to effectively meet the challenge of the 17 million people who are still out of work. such high unemployment is a real threat to the values on which the european social model is based and we must do everything we can to reduce it radically. we have over 60 amendments to the current version of the report. almost half of them support this way of thinking about the report, which is job creation. i hope that the outcome of the vote will be satisfactory enough to allow me to recommend that the house adopt this report and that it will be an important voice in the debate which the european commission launched with the publication of its green paper last november.

mr. chairman, please! labour law is one of the most difficult documents, both in terms of legal and substantive aspects. it contains not only economic and legal elements but also moral ones. and reconciling them is extremely difficult, and sometimes impossible, but we try to reconcile them as much as possible. what should the 21st century labour law be? it should meet, inter alia, the following conditions: first, it should be flexible, allowing it to keep up with rapidly changing conditions. secondly, it should protect and enable employees to develop. third, it should protect the interests of employers and enable firms to develop while maintaining the highest possible efficiency. fourth, it should allow for the optimal use of labour resources. fifth, it should allow for dialogue between workers and employers. and most importantly, labour law must be uniform throughout the european union or applicable in all member states.
mr. chairman, please! it is good that the european parliament has dealt with the problem of labour law in a comprehensive way, and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr protasiewicz, for his report, which is very substantive. the tragic situation of foreign workers in many countries of the european union is also worth mentioning. slave or semi-slave labour camps are being discovered in successive states of the union. people who seek work and bread in other countries are often exploited, humiliated, and sometimes killed by ruthless criminals. this is the shame of the european union in the 21st century. the european parliament should call on the member states and their labour inspection and law enforcement authorities to pay particular attention to the situation of migrant workers and to effectively combat the criminal exploitation of these people.
mr. chairman, please! changes in labour law in the european union are not only important for the safety and security of workplaces, but also have a key impact on employment levels. there has long been a heated debate about whether global competition requires changes to the current model of labour law. i think it is. for the last 20 years, we have seen a gradual and increasingly rapid departure from the standard forms of law and the general model of work. this phenomenon is a response to the challenges of globalisation, which is a process in its own right, and whether we like it or not, it is up to us whether our societies take advantage of the opportunities that this process brings. addressing the negative aspects of globalisation requires much more flexibility in labour law while maintaining the current level of safety. it is worth noting that the current level of occupational safety and health in the european union is among the highest in the world. we do not need further protection of labour, but more flexibility and mobility and the liberalisation of labour markets in all the countries of the european union. regardless of the regulation, flexibility is coming into our lives. today, 40% of all employment forms are customized. moreover, they account for 60% of new jobs, and finally, and this is the most optimistic, two thirds of non-standard forms of employment are moving to the so-called classic form - indefinite contracts. traditional labour law structures do not pass the test in today's realities. in modern service-based economies or in small and medium-sized enterprises, a more flexible and customized approach can be the key to success. of course, flexibility without employee mobility is not enough. i therefore call for the full opening up of the labour markets in the european union to workers from all member states. we now know that the benefits of labour market liberalisation are not limited to migrant workers, but are also very clearly felt by countries that have decided to open up their labour markets. there is no well-developed and competitive economy without well-functioning businesses that can compete in the global marketplace, managed efficiently by good managers, good owners. but there are no companies that do well, even the best-run ones, that don't have very good employees. so these are connected vessels.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i am pleased to present the second report to date of the european parliament in response to the european commission's annual report on the functioning of the eurozone. the commission report presents the economic situation in the euro area in 2007. the evaluations in the report are satisfactory. the euro area's economic growth accelerated to 2.7%, the best since 2000, and unemployment fell to 7.6%, the lowest in 15 years. at the same time, the euro area is increasingly becoming a stabilising factor in the world economy. this generally optimistic picture should not, however, obscure certain negative aspects. we're looking at them in our report. first, the pace of fiscal adjustment is too slow, especially in countries with still large budget deficits. the stability and growth pact requires member states to maintain at least a balanced budget in the medium term. this requires a budget surplus in good times in order to have a financial reserve in times of recession. in this context, we are critical of the behaviour of some member states which do not take advantage of the current period of high growth to make the necessary cuts in public spending. secondly, parliament points out that the good average performance for the euro area as a whole is hidden by significant differences in the economic situation in the individual member states. the decline in the international competitiveness of some countries' economies is particularly worrying, most often due to rapid wage growth outpacing labour productivity growth. thirdly, we call for the continuation of the necessary structural reforms in line with the guidelines contained in the renewed lisbon strategy. the removal of remaining barriers in the markets for goods and services should be accelerated and the further integration of labour and financial markets, which are an important element of the smooth functioning of the euro area, should be promoted. we pay particular attention to the rapid implementation of the services directive, which will help to accelerate labour productivity growth and reduce inflation in the services sector. this is very important because services account for 70% of the euro area's gross domestic product. fourthly, parliament stressed the importance of further enlargement of the euro member of the commission. madam president, members of parliament. i would first of all like to thank mr becsey and parliament’s committee on economic and monetary affairs for the excellent report on the community statistical programme for 2008-2012. this will indeed allow a timely adoption of the legal basis and a smooth start to the programme in 2008. the community statistical programme constitutes the framework for the production of all statistics as well as the financial framework for the production of community statistics during the programme period. statistics are a key element for policy-making and, as such, the new programme has indeed focused on the current priorities of the union, from growth and competitiveness to sustainable development and security. parliament’s amendments, aimed at strengthening the gender and regional dimensions in statistics and substantiating the reporting obligations, are particularly welcomed by the commission. i would therefore like to thank the rapporteur, mr becsey, once again, as well as the committee on regional development for their valuable efforts to provide the community with a solid basis for the production of statistics over the next five years. regarding fiscal statistics and the oral question by mr becsey and mr radwan, the commission certainly agrees that the quality of fiscal data is vital for the correct functioning of economic and monetary union and its budgetary surveillance system as well as for the assessment of the convergence criteria when evaluating the application of a member state for entry into the euro area. fiscal statistics, like any other statistics, are subject to revision. data are routinely revised when new information on government transactions becomes available or when errors or inconsistencies are identified and corrected. revision also takes place in a paramount effort to comply better with the accounting rules. for statisticians, data usually become final only after four years at the earliest. most revisions, in fiscal statistics, are small and have no significant impact on economic analysis and fiscal surveillance. unfortunately, there have also been some episodes of large revisions in fiscal statistics that put fiscal surveillance under stress. however, it is important to note that, in most cases, those revisions have not been a surprise. they were indeed preceded by public statements by eurostat, drawing attention to the fact that the data initially reported by the member states were not in compliance with the accounting rules and requiring member states to amend them. whenever necessary eurostat has even itself amended data reported by the member states. in compliance with regulation 2103/2005, eurostat has reported – and will report regularly to the european parliament and to the council – on the quality of the fiscal data transmitted by member states. with regard to forecasts, the commission regularly assesses the forecasts and projections announced by member states in their stability and convergence programmes by comparing them with the commission’s own forecasts. for several member states, the commission has publicly noted on some occasions that the fiscal forecasts contained in the stability and convergence programmes were based on optimistic macroeconomic projections. the commission has also pointed out cases where the national projections were not compliant with the accounting rules for specific transactions or where the planned policy measures underlying the forecasts had not yet been confirmed. in preparing its own forecasts, the commission systematically compares its numbers with projections released by the imf, the oecd and other organisations. experience shows that the forecasts published by the commission – both the macroeconomic and the fiscal figures – are not biased and are at least as reliable as those of other forecasters.
author of the draft opinion of the committee on regional development. - madam president! - i have to go. i thank mr becsey for his report. i thank you twice, first as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on regional development and secondly as representative of my political group. i'm not going to go into the definition of statistics. i'll just say that it's a science that deals with quantitative methods of studying phenomena and processes of a mass nature. it aims to discover the regularities that govern these phenomena and to quantify them. it allows the results of the analyses to be generalized and the degree of accuracy and reliability of the results to be assessed. i have mentioned this for a reason, because statistics are often the basis for very important decisions, whether at local, regional, national, eu or even global level. it is therefore fortunate that we have a community statistical programme for the years 2008 to 2012. statistics prepared in a reliable and responsible manner are of immense value. therefore, the cost of obtaining them must be appropriate. at this point, i would like to ask the commissioner whether our ambitious programme for the next five years has sufficient financial backing. we are undertaking actions to reach 27 member states with varying levels of experience in this sensitive area. so my second question is: what steps have been or will be taken to ensure the best possible coordination of statistical analysis? the commissioner was kind enough to emphasise the importance of the opinion of the committee on regional development, and i thank her for that complimentary opinion. i would now like to turn to regional issues. the european union, for example, has allocated more than one third of its budget for the 2007-2013 period to a broad regional policy, implementing the principle of cohesion and solidarity between regions with very different levels of prosperity. this money is the money of the european taxpayer and it cannot be wasted in any way. we therefore need to have fully objective, sufficiently comprehensive and reliable methods of monitoring the implementation of structural policies. do we have such methods? this requires the collection and compilation of statistical data, both at community, member state and regional level, as well as at the lower local level. these data must be comparable in nature and dates both within and outside the union, as we often compare ourselves with other countries. it is unacceptable that the achievement of temporary or temporary objectives or technical problems lead to the fact that we have periodic neglect in the collection of statistics. it has fatal consequences. statistical analyses for regions are based on nuts units. the question is, does this division always result in unambiguously reliable data? my reservations are particularly relevant in situations where the level of development and prosperity of the regional capital is clearly higher than that of the rest of the area. the second issue i would like to raise is the question of the development metrics of countries or regions: whether gdp per capita is sufficient, what weight should be given to the unemployment rate, how to assess the quality of life in a given area, and so on. these are important issues, and i know they're not easily resolved. we often talk about innovation in parliament. we should therefore have reliable data in the fields of education, science, research and innovation. the question is: what methods do you use to compare data that often comes from unofficial sources? how do you define the dynamics of change? i would like to raise one more social issue. we are witnessing the changes that are associated with the movement of large numbers of people, especially workers. how does this affect the social status and the status of families? it should also be borne in mind that high statistical reliability always implies trust in the sources of information, which implies confidentiality and often anonymity of the primary data. in conclusion, i would like to express the hope that the community statistical programme will serve the fundamental objectives of the european union well. i am convinced of this both by the attitude of eurostat and by that of the polish central statistical office. i hope so.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - i have to go. i congratulate you on this honourable appointment. the european union is not just 27 countries, but 268 regions that share huge disparities in development. the recent enlargement of the union to 27 countries has increased the population of the community to almost 493 million, of which about 30% live in the 100 poorest regions, the regions covered by the convergence objective. each enlargement has led to greater disparities between the richest and poorest regions of the community. in the union of 27, the differences in gdp between regions are now much greater than they were in the old 15, ranging from 24% in north-eastern romania to 303% in central london. the causes of economic backwardness vary widely from region to region. the poorest regions lack, in particular, the basic infrastructure necessary for sustainable and sustainable development and further investment, and adequate human resources. statistics show that the eu's cohesion policy has so far been effective in promoting the development of many regions in countries that have long been part of it, such as ireland, greece, portugal and spain. in accordance with the community objective, set out in article 158 of the treaty establishing the european community, of the harmonious development and reduction of disparities in the levels of development of the various regions, as the european parliament we call for decisive action to reduce the most acute delays in the development of the poorest regions of the european union. the new member states are particularly hard-pressed to absorb eu funds, as the allocation of funds does not guarantee their proper use, and authorities in poor regions often lack the skills, experience and necessary own resources to make full use of the funds they are entitled to. the procedures for applying for structural fund assistance are often very complex and not entirely transparent to the final recipient. we therefore call for simplification at all levels: european, national and regional. the implementation of cohesion policy should take into account the diverse needs of regions, including in particular urban, rural, hard-to-reach regions, islands, outermost regions, by adapting assistance to their conditions and specific characteristics, while exploiting their potential for sustainable and resilient development. member states and regions should therefore give priority to those projects which contribute to improving accessibility in the poorest regions by providing them with basic transport and telecommunications infrastructure. cohesion policy should support entrepreneurship and investment in the poorest regions. new financial instruments such as jeremy and jessica can make an effective contribution to regional development, but there is still very little awareness of the potential of using them at local and regional level. it is important to encourage member states to establish public-private partnerships and to exchange good practices in this regard. the commission and the member states should effectively support projects that increase the capacity of regions to generate and absorb new technologies, with particular attention to environmental protection. the high unemployment rate of up to 20% is a major problem in the poorest regions of the union. in this context, there is an urgent need to invest in human capital in poor regions through better education, continuous upskilling, especially of young people, women and the elderly, and of vulnerable minorities. promoting equal opportunities for all should be part of every community programme, especially those affecting economic and social cohesion, and at all stages of the design and implementation of projects implemented under the european union's cohesion policy. the commission and the member states should ensure that accurate, complete and comparable statistics are available, which are sadly lacking. the commission should define a new way of measuring regional development, not only on the basis of gdp and unemployment, but also on the basis of other quantitative and qualitative indicators that reflect the real living standards of the population. the method of calculating purchasing power parity should also be improved by developing regional rather than national indicators. on the occasion of the 2009 mid-term review of the community budget, the commission should analyse the effects of cohesion policy and examine the causes of any undesirable outcomes. in conclusion, i would like to thank all those who contributed to this report. i thank you for the valuable amendments that have enriched this document, and i sincerely hope that this own-initiative report will provide useful guidance for the member states and regions and a stimulus for the european commission to improve the effectiveness of cohesion policy in the regions most in need.
madam president! the fourth cohesion report, recently published by the commission, confirms the progress already made in reducing the disparities in development between the richest and poorest regions of europe. assuming that the strongest regions maintain a constant high growth rate, also confirmed by a high innovation burden, it is necessary to consider that the weakest regions show an increased growth rate, not only maintaining the same gap, but even substantially reducing it. these facts confirm the thesis that the european union's cohesion policy is effective and that it needs to be pursued and developed in the following programming periods. the report in question refers to the poorest regions of the european union, not to the poorest regions of the member states, which are often among the relatively richest regions of the european union. interregional disparities at national level are therefore primarily a matter for national authorities and should, especially in the so-called cohesion countries, be supported by european interventions. it requires a distinct and courageous political decision to define which regions we consider to be the poorest and which require specific action to strengthen the pro-development directions. we must remember that the treaty provisions speak of disparities between regions and that cohesion policy must cover not only the poorest regions in terms of gdp per capita but also regions that are distant from others in terms of their level of innovation, the development of the knowledge-based economy, the attractiveness of investment, geographical location and others. as economic growth and the deepening of the common market take place, some disparities may be reduced, but new ones will emerge. cohesion policy has not been and is not a charitable activity and must remain a flexible intervention tool of the european union.

commission. mr president, the commission shares the european parliament’s concern about the violation of human rights in vietnam. this affects, in particular, the exercise of freedom of expression, of association and of religion. however, we must view this in its full context. vietnam has made considerable progress in terms of economic and social rights. over the past decade, it has succeeded in lifting a significant part of its population out of absolute poverty and set the country firmly on a course of economic growth, whilst limiting the emergence of socioeconomic disparities within the population. this has been accompanied by some improvements in recent years in the situation as regards civil and political rights. for instance, new legislation relating to religious freedom, which has been adopted in the last three years, has softened some, but not all, of the tools used by the state to control religious organisations and thus allows non-organised groups to seek official recognition. this has already had a positive impact on the ground. among other things, some protestant denominations, such as baptists and mennonites, which had not been recognised in the past, have been able to register grassroots-level congregations. that said, the implementation of the new legislation remains uneven, and progress in the northern uplands in particular has been markedly slower than in parts of the central highlands and in lowland areas. moreover, some denominations seen as dissident by the regime, such as the unified buddhist church of vietnam, and some hoa hao and cao dai groups, remain illegal and face continued harassment. the climate has also improved for political dissidents in the past two years. a considerable number of high-profile activists were released in 2005 and 2006. last year also saw the emergence of some new parties and other groupings of activists within the country, which was unprecedented both in terms of the number of groups and of that of their adherents. the official reaction to this development was, initially, relatively low-key. however, this changed in early 2007, and in particular since mid-february. harassment of dissidents seems to have intensified, and scores of activists were arrested. a number of them have since been tried and sentenced to lengthy jail terms. this includes some well-known persons such as father nguyen van ly, and lawyers nguyen van dai and le thi cong nhan. we do not know whether this is a temporary reflex or something more deep-seated, but it is of grave concern to the commission. the eu’s relations with vietnam have developed dynamically in recent years, and the commission has taken every opportunity to press for continued improvement in the human rights situation, especially as regards prisoners of concern. the commission and eu member states’ representatives in hanoi have in particular followed the recent arrests and trials of activists with particular attention. eu diplomats were present at some of the trials as observers, and the eu reacted strongly to their sentencing. in its declaration of 15 may, it reiterated its plea to the government of vietnam to release all non-violent political activists exercising their rights to freedom of expression and association. the eu missions in hanoi have also requested that the vietnamese government allow them to visit dissidents in prison, in order to ascertain the conditions of their detention. the recent trials were also raised forcefully by commissioner ferrero-waldner in her bilateral meeting with vietnamese deputy prime minister khiem on 28 may 2007, on the margins of the asem ministerial meeting in hamburg. apart from high-level political contacts, the eu and vietnam have agreed on mechanisms to conduct a dialogue and exchange of views on human rights issues. a key instrument in this regard is the regular human rights dialogue between the eu missions in hanoi and the government of vietnam. the sub-group on cooperation in the areas of institution building, administrative reform, governance and human rights provides another opportunity for the commission to raise these issues. on all possible occasions, we have expressed our view that the arrest of non-violent political activists is incompatible with vietnam’s obligations under the international human rights instruments to which it has acceded. please rest assured that the commission will continue to use all instruments at its disposal to press the case in question, as well as, more generally, to encourage and support progress on human rights and religious freedom in vietnam. we also rely very much on the european parliament to continue to press for the improvement of human rights in vietnam.

on behalf of the uen group. - madam president! - i have to go. in taking part in the debate on better lawmaking in the european union on behalf of the uen group, i would like to draw attention to the following points. first, the authors of the report support a better lawmaking process aimed at making union law more effective, efficient, coherent and transparent, which, in my view, should be carried out under the following conditions:- the council, the commission and the european parliament must act together on this matter;- a broad and open consultation of all interested parties, including - i would like to stress this in particular - businesses, local governments and non-governmental organisations, should be carried out on this matter;- the responsibility of the community institutions for the lawmaking process should be increased and the overall transparency of the process improved;- any change in the law that aims to simplify it must, however, take into account equally the social, environmental and economic considerations as well as the health and safety of the legal process concerned;- it should not lead to a lowering of the standards of law in the union. secondly, the authors also point out that the draft legislation should avoid vague and unnecessary language and use simple and understandable language, while maintaining precise terminology and legal certainty, so that union law can be understood by almost 500 million citizens. thirdly, it is welcome that the 2007 spring summit of the council of the union adopted a decision to reduce the administrative burden arising from community law by 25% by 2012. it is only to be hoped that this objective will be more realistic than the lisbon objectives. fourthly, it should also be underlined that the reports also suggested alternative solutions to the introduction of new legislation, such as self-regulation or mutual recognition of national rules, or even the option of not taking any legislative action. all of them deserve special attention in a situation of enormous inflation of eu law.

madam president! better regulation is of great importance for harmonising action in the european union. i would like to thank all the rapporteurs for their very good reports: katalina lévai, bert doorn, giuseppe gargani, manuel medina ortedze. in many national parliaments, and in ours, there is a tendency to legislate on as many issues as possible. in many cases, this is because of the way people think that making a rule will solve the problem. and we want to take into account all the parties' reasons, the lobbyists, the vested interests. legislation becomes less transparent and accessible to citizens, businesses and administrations. they become voluminous, opaque and difficult to transpose in all countries. better law-making should use legislative instruments to achieve the objectives set out in the treaty. co-regulation and self-regulation can complement legislative measures, but only if these methods offer an improvement of a scope equivalent to or greater than that of legislation. the lack of legal coverage and better regulation are not new problems, but require the quickest possible action. assessment of the legislative effects, preservation of terminological precision and legal certainty, reduction of abbreviations and overly lengthy preambles should contribute to better, more modern, rational and effective legislation. the measures taken will significantly reduce the administrative costs for parliament, the parties and the users of the law. another issue is the application of the 'soft law' based on community practice. it does not provide full legal protection, is not binding and raises legal concerns. madam president! dura lex - sed lex, is one of those latin maxims that i'm sure most lawyers know very well. hard law, but law. today we're focusing on a soft law that sets a direction, but it's not a legally binding act. it shall express political declarations, resolutions, council declarations and presidency conclusions, but shall not be binding. however, it may also be used by the european court of justice for the interpretation of the provisions. it is therefore a law, although the court states that it is not intended to be binding even on those to whom it is addressed. in practice, however, national courts are obliged to take the recommendations into account when resolving disputes. they help to interpret national law which has been adopted to ensure its application or to supplement binding community legislation. the rapporteur is very critical of non-binding legislation, and in particular of the commission's misapplication of it. stresses that, where the community has legislative power, it would be appropriate for an act to be adopted by institutions such as the council or the parliament, taking into account the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality; i agree with the rapporteur that only by adopting legislation within the framework of the institutional procedures and those mentioned in the treaty will it be possible to guarantee the enforceability and enforceability of the law.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i am very grateful for the broad consensus that has emerged in this debate, but i would like to clarify a few things again. first, better regulation is not deregulation. i must fight it with all my might. this is not a deregulation commission, but, as i said, european integration is based on the law and not on the abolition of the law. better regulation is exactly what the name says: it is about making it better, more modern, simpler, more transparent, with more consideration above all for the needs of small and mediumsized enterprises, on which we often impose the same burdens as on large corporations, and that is unfair. i would like to confirm to mrs frassoni that this is not about lowering standards. if you look at the many initiatives that the commission has put forward so far, you will find that in no single case has the commission proposed to lower a standard or to weaken the level of european integration that has been achieved. it is always a question of achieving the objectives which you - the european parliament - consider politically necessary by simpler, more modern and cheaper means. i want to make this explicitly clear. there is a great deal of confusion about the numbers. i'm a little surprised. so, as far as simplification is concerned, it is an ongoing programme that is constantly being supplemented. the commission has so far 143 simplification initiatives under way, of which about half have already been adopted; 67 initiatives have already been adopted. these initiatives naturally always cover a whole range of basic acts with subsequent legislation. so if we say we have 143 simplification initiatives, that means that several thousand pieces of legislation are affected. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is quite clear that after 50 years of european integration, something like this must be done. the question of cost is a different matter. mr helmer's assertions do not become true by being repeated over and over again. he's probably not here, but i'd like to make this clear once and for all. administrative burdens on businesses are defined as costs incurred by european businesses due to documentation, statistical and information requirements and as a consequence of european, national or regional legislation. they amount to a total of 3.5% of european gross national product, but for all three levels: european, national and regional. we have already seen how this is divided: about 35% of these costs come directly from european legislation, 15% come from national implementation of european legislation and the remaining 50% are purely national. it is, of course, wrong for mr helmer to say that the eu is costing the economy 350 billion euros, that the benefits of the single market are not so great, and that the costs to the eu would exceed the benefits of the single market. i am sorry, but this is a farmer's game and it is aimed at the stupidity of the people, because it ignores the fact that if there is no eu law, there is national law. in the united kingdom, too, we know that there is a particularly high level of unemployment. it would certainly be more expensive. i will give you just one example of the enormous simplifications and savings that can be made in european legislation. we had 1 400 different regulations in 27 member states in the field of technical regulations for radio equipment in europe. this means that a company in the uk that made certain radio equipment had to know 1,400 national regulations. this parliament followed the commission's proposal and adopted a regulation which merged these 1 400 regulations into one. it is not possible to calculate the cost savings for the company, but it is obvious. the 25% reduction is absolutely achievable. we have provided the 10 fast-track actions with the proposal to show that it is technically relatively simple. all you have to do is to look at the existing regulations to see what statistical, information and documentation obligations there are and whether we need them at all - given the practice we have now - to that extent. the result is often that they are not needed at all or that modern information and communication technologies make it all much easier. we shall reach that 25%, and it will lead to a productivity gain of 1.5% of gross national product for the european economy. this has a macroeconomic dimension, of course, because there are not many economic programmes in the european union that have a positive growth effect of 1.5%. i would like to say this in passing: if all goes well, we will also achieve a very high growth effect when the new transatlantic cooperation removal of trade barriers in transatlantic trade is successfully concluded. we have attached importance to this clarification so that we know what we are talking about. i would like to emphasize all that has been said here about the importance of impact assessment. this is the a and o, and the commission's rule is: no new proposal without a comprehensive impact assessment and no new proposal without an impact assessment which has been examined by the impact assessment board. if this has been violated on occasion, i believe that the european parliament has the absolute right, if not the duty, to criticise it. without an impact assessment, the legislator is unable to assess the actual consequences of his action. even if an impact assessment shows that a new proposal has a cost to the economy or to the citizens, this does not mean that the measure is not implemented, because there are things more important than costs. when it comes to preserving our environment, fighting climate change, reducing our dependence on fossil fuels or the health of our citizens, it's not a matter of cost. then we must do what is necessary. the commission feels, however, that it is its duty to give parliament full information on the social, environmental and economic consequences of any new proposal. that's why impact assessment is so crucial. we shall examine very carefully the proposals made here. the most important thing that has been said several times in this debate is the following, and i fully agree with it: all this can only succeed as a joint project. it cannot succeed if we see it as a conflict between the institutions, but only if all three institutions, parliament, the council and the commission, want it together and declare it their priority together. only then will it work.

member of the commission. mr president, i am dealing with this file on behalf of my colleague, mrs kroes, the competition commissioner. the commission is not seeking the closure of gdansk shipyard. gdansk shipyard has played a crucial part in european history and in the struggle for freedom and a reunited europe. we would like to see the yard undertaking a genuine far-reaching restructuring so as to become a successful company capable of competing on its own merits in the eu and world shipbuilding markets. in the last decades, the shipbuilding industry has restructured all around europe. the commission is well aware that for many yards and regions this has been a difficult process. many shipyards were closed and the shipbuilding capacity had to be reduced. wherever national state aid has been used for this restructuring, the commission has had to exercise its responsibility under the treaty to ensure that the level playing field among shipbuilders in the european union was not distorted. the commission now has the same responsibility concerning its intervention in the gdansk case. the conditions under which state aid for ailing companies is compatible with the treaty are clearly set out in the community guidelines on state aid for rescuing and restructuring firms in difficulties. the proper restructuring of gdansk shipyard has been postponed for many years; public money has not been used to create viable jobs, but to keep alive a company that would under normal market conditions have ceased to exist. the commission's goals here are three-fold. first, to ensure that the restructuring of gdansk shipyard leads to its own long-term viability. it could possibly mean scaling down its activities, but would eventually lead to the emergence of a smaller but more efficient shipyard capable of standing on its own feet. second, to limit the distortion of the level playing field and any harm to european competitors caused by state intervention, the yard's production capacity has to be reduced. also, a significant contribution to the restructuring plan must be made from own resources, including the sale of assets that are not essential to the shipyard's survival, or from external financing at market conditions. third, to ensure equal treatment. shipyards in other countries as well as other polish shipyards, have had to reduce considerably their capacity. gdansk shipyard cannot be an exception. structural funds and other eu assistance have been used by other member states to tackle the difficult transition period and to support the affected regions. we have repeatedly reminded the polish authorities of this possibility. the commission has been, and will remain, in close and constructive dialogue with the polish authorities to seek a way forward in which the conditions for compatibility of the state aid are met and the state aid can be approved. that process is ongoing. gdansk shipyard deserves a viable future by developing a new and sustainable position in the competitive shipbuilding industry of the eu.

member of the commission. madam president, first of all let me refer to the accident that ms fraga estévez and ms miguélez ramos mentioned. i share their concern and sorrow at the loss of life and hope that the missing fishermen can be brought to safety. allow me to pick up on some of the points that were raised in the debate, which have proved to be quite varied to say the least – poles apart on how to move forward. however, having said that, from the debate it is clear that we share a common view that fisheries have to be brought to sustainable levels as soon as possible. this does not mean that what we are proposing is drastic and immediate action. rather we are setting ourselves an objective to arrive at maximum sustainable yield (msy) in a gradual and flexible manner. at each step we will re-evaluate and re-assess the targets we set and if required, we will adapt them to changing situations. in other word, the msy approach is providing us with a direction and not necessarily with a fixed target. let me repeat, the msy approach moves fisheries management in the right direction, away from over-exploitation and towards conditions of higher and more stable catches and lower costs. this approach should be adaptive so that as we learn more – or, as environmental and ecosystem conditions change – new knowledge can be applied to the approach. the point has been raised that msy has not worked and is not appropriate for pelagic stocks, and that it is an outdated concept. let me say there have been fisheries management strategies in europe and in other parts of the world which were successful. although the concept is not new, it does not mean that it is outdated. the important point is that, as long as it defines a path for fisheries management and is flexible enough to allow for regular revisions, it has good chances of success. good examples of some success can be seen in stocks such as saithe, north sea haddock and mackerel, which are fished close to msy level and which are generally stable and profitable. let me highlight one point. the purpose of this proposal is not to penalise fishermen, who, admittedly, have to make a number of adjustments, but rather it seeks to reach an objective and embark on a direction where the sector operates in a more stable and in a more profitable environment. as i stated in my opening statement, the european fisheries fund allows member states to develop measures concerning adjustments of capacity and fishing effort in the context of long-term plans, including social and economic provisions involving the appropriate use of public money, in their operational programmes. another point raised relates to the fact that msy will not work in mixed fisheries, because when targeting one stock to move towards msy one could end up in a situation where the other stocks caught in such a mixed fishery are under-exploited. i think we have to be realistic about the situation and the majority of mixed fisheries. the stocks concerned are equally exploited to unsustainable levels. it is clear that the application of the msy approach to mixed fisheries will be difficult and will have to be studied on a case-by-case basis. however, the mixed fisheries problem exists and, if we do not address it, there can be no improvements and no steps can be taken in the right direction. regarding consultation, let me say that the commission is committed to stakeholder involvement and consultation. many consultations have already been held since the adoption of the objective of msy at the johannesburg summit. such consultations involved member states, scientists and the regional advisory councils, who are studying our proposal as well and who are seeking to advise us on the best way forward. discussions on the plans will be held at a later stage, after we have developed impact assessments, consulted the industry and drawn up our specific proposals. i look forward to a continued dialogue with you on these plans.

compromise formula, since it is now expected that the commission will include in its report an analysis of the prospects for opening up domestic markets to competition. it will do so taking into account the experience gained in the application of the public service regulations as well as differences between member states. and, mr jarzembowski, if necessary, the commission will propose in its report additional measures to facilitate the gradual opening up of the market. i am aware that this compromise should have been more ambitious for you, but it has two advantages. it allows us to implement the new legislative framework, including public services. it also provides a clear and timely perspective for a detailed analysis of the impact of this new legislative framework in all member states. we will then be able to examine the appropriateness of further proposals from the commission. the second point of the negotiation was the public service financing charge. a number of member states have requested that all rail services in their territories, whether national or international, and regardless of the providers of these services, all rail services contribute to the financing of public services in passenger transport, subject to the levying of a fee. when the council adopted the common position, the commission accepted this possibility in so far as it was compatible with community law. the compromise reached in the conciliation committee thus incorporated several elements of parliament's second reading. i thank your parliamentary delegation for joining us and i confirm my commitment to being able to complete this legislative framework as far as possible. i come now, mr savary, to the certification of the flight crew. apart from some more or less technical questions, which were easily resolved before the final meeting, two issues remained to be resolved: firstly, the partial reimbursement of training costs when a driver leaves a company prematurely, and secondly, the scope of the directive. for the partial reimbursement of training costs, the solution was to ask the member states to solve this problem by means of national solutions, since, in the end, a harmonization of the solutions was not necessary. as far as the scope is concerned, i think we have found the best solution. the european railway agency will undertake a more in-depth study on the profile and tasks of staff on board trains that contribute to their safety. this will enable us to develop a more targeted proposal for these staff, but you have done well in stressing the extreme importance of this issue of the certification of flight crew. i come now, mr sterckx, to the rights and obligations of rail passengers. the final phase of the negotiations focused on the scope of the regulation on rail passengers' rights. parliament has from the outset wanted the charges to be levied on all rail services, including national services. but a large number of member states saw major difficulties in applying it, particularly to local services, which have characteristics very different from international or long distance services. the final solution has two essential elements: a new distinction between services and significant transition periods. the new structure organises the scope around long and short distance parameters, with the short distance covering urban, suburban and regional services. the regulation therefore no longer refers to 'national' and 'international' travellers. this new situation, to which you have made a great contribution, mr sterckx, has enabled us to reach agreement on the most difficult point of the negotiations. the scope of the solution chosen has many advantages: greater conformity with the internal market compared with the parameters originally envisaged, this national and international dimension; the commission will be able to take account of the size and structure of the territory in an objective manner when defining urban, suburban and regional services at national level within the framework established by the regulation. the compromise also postponed the application of certain chapters of the regulation for a transitional period of five years, renewable twice. this solution makes it possible to ease the burden on railway companies immediately, while maintaining the obligation to transpose the duties established by the regulation. the railway companies will therefore not be able to relax their efforts in the future. i would also remind you that the regulation will contain a minimum set of duties, applicable as soon as it comes into force and without any possible exemption. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the railway system is not affected by the accident. that's a lot of money. this is a good result, which will make it possible to offer a much better service to rail passengers in the future. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have shown that together we can make things happen. of course, this is just a phase. we must now ensure that the rules adopted by parliament and the council are properly applied. the commission, in its role as guardian of the treaties, will not relent in its efforts to do so. with the slight delay due to my arrival by direct train from cyprus, i was unable to hear the three rapporteurs, but i understood what mr savary said about the absolute necessity of this interoperability for the europeanisation of railways. at this price we will be able to transfer part of the freight to rail, the benefits of which are now being fully appreciated, particularly in view of our priority in the fight against global warming. it is true that this package is imperfect, but it has the great merit of being here, of existing, and i cannot thank enough, mr president, all the members who have contributed to its adoption, which also marks a new stage for us, and to which i will be personally very committed and very vigilant.

rapporteur. – madam president, i am presenting to you an own-initiative report recommended by an overwhelming majority in the committee on foreign affairs. our report advocates a common eu foreign policy on energy in order to face challenges of energy security. it would bring necessary and substantial added value to efforts made at national level, according to the subsidiarity principle, and would allow better protection of europe’s energy interests. what should this policy look like? it should be based on the following four principles: diversification; unity in defending the eu’s interests and the eu speaking with one voice; solidarity in crisis; and strengthened cooperation with partners. we need to develop a proactive broad energy diplomacy aimed at strengthening our cooperation with all major producer, transit and consumer countries, and to create an energy market based on the principle of reciprocity. the report welcomes the proposals of the third energy package, as adopted last week by the commission, which addresses these concerns and is in line with the report. the eu has to be active, determined and united. the geopolitical dimension of energy security has been so far neglected and it is high time to fill the gap. hopefully the new treaty will equip the eu with a legal basis for energy solidarity, thus allowing for the eu’s institutional competence to negotiate an energy security framework with third countries. the report recommends including in our agreements with producer and transit countries a so-called energy security clause which lays down a code of conduct and explicitly outlines measures to be taken in the event of disruption of supply. we should replace the current eu member states’ preference for energy unilateralism with a new common policy of energy solidarity based on a multilateralist approach. meanwhile, there is a necessity to establish a good practice of consultation among member states on strategic decisions which may affect the eu or one of its members. the new common foreign policy on energy must be consistent with all eu policies having an external aspect, e.g. internal market, competition, transport, trade, environment, consumer protection, budget and others. one cannot create a new common policy overnight. we propose, therefore, to adopt a gradual approach and furthermore, to be efficient, this new policy should be equipped with appropriate instruments. we suggest the creation of a new post of high official for foreign energy policy after the new treaty enters – hopefully – into force. this office would allow for the coordination of all the above-mentioned sectoral policies of the union and especially those aspects related to the external side of energy security, working under the authority of the high representative for the common foreign and security policy, who would, in future, also be vice-president of the european commission. that would reinforce the synergies inside the union. this institutional novelty therefore constitutes an important anchorage of the new approach. we also propose to elaborate a precise roadmap indicating short-, medium- and long-term objectives with a specific timeframe for implementing them and obviously subject to the european parliament’s scrutiny. to be successful, we need to engage the eu’s internal dynamic and to secure the necessary public support. the citizens’ interest is in secure and affordable energy. this interest of our citizens should be at the core of the project, thus constituting one of the targets of our ‘europe of results’ approach. common threats to secure energy for europe should therefore produce a common response. but we may also achieve more: a new common policy can become a trigger for further european integration, giving it a new impetus and new strength to the eu as a global actor. a demanding and courageous approach should be an ambition of the european parliament. today’s european union started a long time ago with energy. then, it was coal giving an initial push to our reconstruction. we should not miss the opportunity to let it happen once again. we need energy for europe, indeed, both in literal and in metaphorical terms.
on behalf of the uen group. we have a great opportunity for a common energy policy. the commission's latest communication shows that we are on the right track. the report by mr saryusz-wolski is also an important step in this direction. firstly, we have a proper presentation of energy trade issues in the context of foreign policy. the european union has long avoided this. it was only russia's hostile energy policy that made us realize that energy trade had become a purely political instrument. the report includes energy security among the union's security priorities. we have a well-defined principle of solidarity and a requirement for diversification of suppliers and transmission corridors. we have legitimate doubts about the northern gas pipeline, the need for russia to respect the principles of the energy charter, to be involved in the wto and to extend our energy policy beyond the context of the member states of the european union. for all these reasons, our political group is eager to support this report. i congratulate the rapporteur!

madam president! this excellent report by jacques saryusz-wolski shows that security of supply is the most important aspect of the union's energy policy today. already today, half of our dependence on foreign suppliers is as high as 57 percent for gas and 82 percent for oil. this means that any crisis between the supplier and the european union, or between the supplier and the transit country, can have a disastrous impact on our economies and our citizens. it is therefore all the more important to introduce the principle of solidarity between member states in the event of crises into our legal order with the reform treaty. however, in order to ensure that this principle is respected in practice, it is necessary to set up a system of strategic reserves, to increase the number of links between transmission networks and to set up a well-functioning response mechanism to provide technical assistance to the countries most affected by crises. solidarity between the member states must also be reflected in the common external energy policy, and it is good that the commission is assuring us of its willingness to develop such a policy, as we heard from commissioner piebalgs. the member states must be persuaded to abandon their particularism in favour of a common approach and the common good. it is important that this policy be based on the principle of diversification of both sources and suppliers, and finally of energy supply routes and methods. this means that new infrastructure projects such as the odessa-brody-płock pipeline and the nabucco gas pipeline need political and financial support. but it also obliges us to oppose projects that divide the community, such as the baltic gas pipeline. finally, the european union's energy clauses should become a permanent migration is not just a problem in southern europe. it applies to the whole of the union, including poland, my country, which is in the north-east of the continent. poland's eastern border is the longest land border in the union, and we are responsible for keeping it sealed. frontex is also in warsaw, and we expect so much from it. we have given frontex tasks and responsibilities, so we should also provide it with the means and tools to be able to act and protect our borders well. in recent years, almost 3 million of my countrymen have left poland, taking advantage of the rules of the common market and moving to the countries of the european union. but we also have thousands of visitors from the far east: koreans, vietnamese, not to mention ukrainians and belarusians. we need them, they're building poland. i therefore welcome the reports by lilla gruber and sánchez, especially the report on immigration policy, because its aim is to civilize immigration by creating channels for legal immigration. these two reports complement each other perfectly. if we add to this the directive on criminal sanctions for the employment of illegal immigrants, which the libe committee is currently working on, we have a good legal basis for eu immigration policy. i am glad that parliament is playing such a big role here. and one last note: please don't look at immigration as a problem. let us see immigration as an opportunity for an ageing europe! let us use the enthusiasm and energy of the people who come to us legally, let us involve them in the construction of new states and our common europe!
mr. chairman, please! it's worth noting the distribution of accents in the report on illegal migration. this report focuses primarily on the mediterranean basin. secondly, it puts too much faith in community instruments. we all know that the responsibility for border control lies with the member states. and in this respect, despite the appeal to the principle of solidarity or the existence of frontex, much still depends on the readiness of the specific services of the member state. that's why a balanced approach to immigration policy is so important. the situation at the east-south land border also requires attention, funding and joint action, even if this direction is currently less attractive to illegal migrants. the enlargement of the schengen area may, in turn, exacerbate the problems of emigration. this is why the union's policy on legal migration is so important. however, to manage legal labour migration, we must first address the exploitation of the potential and mobility of labour within the union. the existence of transitional periods for the opening of labour markets to nationals of new member states, or the selective abolition of such periods by opening them only to highly qualified workers, seriously undermines any ideas of a community emigration policy towards third-country nationals. the cultural and geographical aspect of legal migration is also important. it is natural that member states, because of their geographical location, cultural and linguistic proximity, prefer certain third countries with which they wish to conduct migration policies. these are countries with which, through proximity, familiarity, or even a language, it is easier for their citizens to integrate with european culture and values. that's why this kind of legal emigration has a double added value.

possible because we will need european rules. it's clear that immigration brings us a universal value, some have said: the mobility of people. i believe that there are opportunities, but also rights, and rights are always accompanied by duties! we cannot imagine a policy which looks at rights and does not look at duties. we cannot and will not impose our europe, our laws or our finances on someone else's house if our partners do not agree. and so here is what we should make very clear, that our idea, our policy is that of a partnership, is that of a grand pact with the countries from which immigrants come through which immigrants transit. this pact must include the absolute respect - and it is an essential component - on our territory of our laws, our fundamental rights, our most absolute and universal values: the european union is a great example of this. and that leads to integration. integration of immigrants means respect for their history, their religion, because they are sources of enrichment for all of you, but it also means respect for our traditions, our history, our culture and our religion. that's why integration, as i see it, is participation. we cannot legally integrate those who do not want to integrate, those who are not ready to take a step forward, those who think that forced marriages or polygamy can still be tolerated in europe. this cannot be accepted because it is our law and it is our universal values. that is why we are calling for the establishment of a european community which is not only a european community but also a european community of the people. this is steadfastness against the lawless. some people have said that, but i particularly share this thought: it is the immigrants who commit crimes who are the worst enemies of the honest immigrants who work and earn regularly. because we have to explain this as a policy, to citizens who are concerned, that they should not be afraid of immigration as such, but of those who commit crimes. we have a duty to ensure that those who commit crimes are punished, because otherwise we do not give any signal of difference to the citizens and we leave this fear, this concern, which then becomes racism and becomes xenophobia, which is a horrible but growing phenomenon in the territory of the european union, uncontrolled. in conclusion, mr president, politics has to make choices. i believe that our choice must be a global pact of rights and duties between equals, between equal partners, with no one imposing and the other accepting, nor reciprocal impositions that we cannot accept. and that is necessary because we are talking about human beings, about their dignity, about their rights. we are not talking about a recipe for economic growth or a recipe for bureaucracy.
in writing. illegal immigration is a rather paradoxical term. i grew up in a political system where certain words were dictated by the government and propaganda was considered a priori positive or negative, like internationalism was good and cosmopolitanism was bad. i hope we don't fall into a similar semantic trap. if xenophobia is bad, then protecting a country or the european union from illegal immigration shouldn't be seen as a very good thing. it's more of a necessary evil. in my city, poznan, i saw a sign on the wall that said, "no one is illegal". it's worth thinking about whether a man can be illegal at all. the deadly danger of crossing the union's borders is not limited to the atlantic and the mediterranean. last week, three chechen girls died at the ukrainian-polish border, as they fled with their mother from a tragedy that had struck their homeland. no wonder people are trying to escape chechnya, even at the risk of losing their lives. the several million immigrants in europe who have come to the union illegally are a very real problem. but in solving this problem, we must remember the universal values that underpin european integration. we also need to remember that immigration is not a negative thing. for one simple reason: man is not a negative thing.
in writing. mr. chairman, please! the eit concept has been evolving in the course of a lively debate on how to promote innovation in the european union. it was originally intended to be the european equivalent of the massachusetts institute of technology, as part of the lisbon agenda, a strategy to compete with the united states. today, in a rapidly changing global environment, it is more about a network of knowledge and innovation centres, kics, coordinated by the central government. this was reflected in the separation of two budget lines in the amendments tabled by the european parliament to the 2008 draft budget (separate funding of the network and the coordinating body). the problem of financing this project seems close to being solved, since the european commission has proposed a revision of the financial perspective 2007-2013, namely raising the ceiling in heading 1a, with reductions in other headings. this is further proof that parliament was right to signal that the budgetary appropriations for the lisbon strategy were too low. i support the ambitions of wroclaw, which is vying for the seat of the european institute of technology. however, i would point out that better r & d funding and the creation of a new institution are not sufficient prerequisites for europe's competitiveness and innovation. the business culture, the willingness to take risks and the practical links between r & d and private enterprise are decisive.
