on behalf of the pse group. - madam president! - i have to go. the proposal for a directive on the legal protection of industrial designs in question concerns the liberalisation of the aftermarket for spare parts for the automotive industry, which is estimated to be worth eur 10 billion across the union. the common market currently covers only the sale of new cars and most member states maintain in their legal systems their own provisions protecting designs and models of visible spare parts. this means that the production and trade of parts such as engine covers, doors, bumpers and mudguards cannot take place freely and different regulations in this field in different member states distort competition. in countries with full design protection, such as austria, france, germany and the czech republic, the prices of spare parts are on average 6 to 10% higher. the main beneficiaries are the european consumer and small and medium-sized enterprises that would like to enter the market and compete fairly with authorised services. opponents of liberalization are mainly large car companies, who believe that independent manufacturers will sell parts at a lower price because they do not bear the costs of designing and developing a new product. the commission proposal is another step towards the full liberalisation of the automotive market in europe. the repair clause is a consumer-friendly law, opposes the monopoly of car groups on the spare parts market and affects greater competition between manufacturers, resulting in lower prices for parts and higher quality. it is worth noting that the repair clause has already been introduced with positive effects for consumers in 11 competitive and high-growth countries of the european union, including ireland, the united kingdom and, among the new members of the union, latvia, hungary and poland. in fact, the only difference between the parts of independent producers and the ones with the group logo is usually the packaging. 80% of the parts are produced by independent producers and only 20% are produced directly by the groups. the protection of designs has nothing to do with the safety of the parts, but only with their appearance, as has been confirmed by reliable analyses carried out so far throughout europe. in conclusion, i would like to add that the five-year period is the maximum that european consumers can agree to.
on behalf of the uen group. - madam president! - i have to go. the subject of today's debate is the liberalization of the spare parts market. the idea is to allow manufacturers other than the owners of the car companies to produce spare parts for cars. mr lehne's report is going in a very good direction and both i personally and the group of the union for a europe of nations support the conclusions drawn from it. we realize, i realize, as a supporter of a liberal economy, that for a good and efficient liberal economy, two elements are essential: on the one hand, the freedom to produce and sell various products, and on the other hand, the protection of the property of the producer, the original producer, his intellectual property, you could say his copyright. but the point is that complete economic freedom will not be effective if we do not respect the property of the person who gave the first idea and who has, as it were, a moral right to that product, who invented it and who is its original owner. on the other hand, there is no economic freedom if copyright leads to market monopoly and thus restricts economic freedom. i am convinced that in this area, in the field of spare parts, in those countries where there have been restrictions in favour of the copyright of the original manufacturer, there has been a de facto restriction of the economy, an increase in the price of the product and thus a monopoly of the car manufacturer, and therefore of the owner of intellectual property. so if we want to balance the law of any market on the one hand, and the right to preserve intellectual property on the other, we have to put some boundaries on that intellectual property. i think that this report is moving in that direction and that is why, from the point of view of economic liberalism, that is to say, the system which produces the most efficient, the most productive and the best production, if it is kept within certain limits, i support the report and congratulate mr lehne on it.

mr president, the lisbon treaty will have a significant impact on the foreign policy of the european union in the coming future. our discussions in the committee on foreign affairs in this house allow me to pronounce a very positive view on the new treaty for a number of reasons. a single framework greatly enhances the coherence of the eu’s external action: the new treaty implies a major step forward when compared to the existing arrangements. it provides an explicitly legal basis for the neighbourhood policy, establishes a single legal personality of the union as a whole and obliges member states to consult one another and to demonstrate mutual solidarity. in the institutional aspect, major improvements are made by enhancing the powers of the double-hatted high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security who is at the same time vice-president of the european commission and by establishing the european external action service. most importantly, the new treaty enhances the budgetary powers of parliament over eu foreign policy spending, putting the european parliament on an equal footing with the council. moreover, the new legal basis for instruments or policies related to the common foreign and security policy (cfsp) are also established, for instance the sanctions against non-state entities, space policy and energy security, combating climate change, prevention of international terrorism and protection of personal data. in fact, the greatest improvements refer to the european security and defence policy (esdp), since the lisbon treaty provides in particular for a permanent structured cooperation in defence between those member states with the military capability. from our point of view, however, the new treaty also suffers from a few shortcomings: the european parliament should be consulted on the nomination of the new high representative and vice-president of the commission, not only for the first person to take office on 1 january 2009, but also in the case of the interim appointment afterwards and, obviously, when appointing the whole commission, including its vice-president for foreign affairs. let me also highlight the need for the new, newly-elected high representative and vice-president to effectively consult parliament ex ante on the main aspects of the basic choices of cfsp and esdp. to sum up: the lisbon treaty constitutes a milestone in the institutional development of the european union in foreign affairs and, as chairman of the committee on foreign affairs, i would like to warmly welcome its pending signature.

in writing. mr. chairman, please! the internal market is a very complex structure which has for many years successfully balanced the interests of the various groups dependent on it. the aim of this directive is to fully liberalise the aftermarket for spare parts. on the one hand, there are therefore a large number of manufacturers of spare parts who are demanding that their rights in the field of free competition and the prohibition of monopolies be respected, and on the other hand, there are car manufacturers (with particular reference to the car industry, of course) who, when investing in new car brands, argue that their spare parts are protected by the right to protection of designs. in this situation, which at first sight seems hopeless, i share the approach of the rapporteur, who proposes a system of temporary limitation of design protection. in practice, the term of protection of a design would be strictly based on the life cycle of the design of the complex product. i also agree with the rapporteur that, when a new protected design is introduced, the old design loses the protection of the design of the spare parts for the previous design, and it also ends when the production of the design in question, without a replacement design, ends. i think that is the most appropriate proposal and the one that best protects the interests of the groups involved. i also support the proposed transitional solution whereby member states whose existing legislation provides for design protection may apply such protection for five years from the entry into force of the directive.

member of the commission. madam president, i welcome today’s debate about the eu-china human rights dialogue. as you know, the human rights issue was raised and discussed at the very recent summit progress in the human rights field over the last year. this is particularly true in the field of social and economic rights but also in some other areas. there are moves afoot to reform the ‘re-education through labour’ system. in this respect we welcome the new legislative initiative that is under consideration and we also hope that concrete reforms will be put in place soon. it is a fundamental principle of human rights not to deprive an individual of his or her liberty without due justice and a fair trial. china is also working to implement the recommendations of the un special rapporteur on torture. for example, the ministry of justice has recently directed courts not to rely on confessions on their own as sufficient evidence of guilt, as such confessions can sometimes be made as a result of torture by police or detention personnel. similarly, china is initiating specific training measures targeted at these groups of public order personnel. we are also pleased to note the progress made with respect to the supreme people’s court now exercising full review power over death penalty sentences issued by lower courts. and we understand that the result is a reduction in the number of effective death sentences and executions. this is gratifying for the european union. as you know, it has long been a priority area of intervention. nevertheless – and now of course i also have to say a few negative things – the commission remains concerned by the situation of human rights in china in general and more specifically in the field of civil and political rights. we particularly have in mind here freedom of expression, religion and association and the protection of the rights of minorities, for instance in tibet and in the province of xinjiang. in this context, the repression of human rights defenders remains a key concern. exercising the right to speak freely often leads to beatings, to house arrest or even to terms of imprisonment. access to the internet – the right to information – is closely monitored and restricted and those, for instance, who speak up in favour of greater autonomy for tibet receive disproportionately long terms of imprisonment. the use of state secrecy legislation as well as other loosely defined criminal provisions facilitates the prosecution of those who speak or publish freely. the commission therefore urges the chinese government to permit expressions of all forms of opinion. this is also, we think, a very important factor for how the international public views china, particularly next year in the run-up to the olympics, when all eyes will be on china. history shows that allowing freedom of expression leads, in the long term, to a far more stable society. we all know that. all these issues are regularly addressed in the eu-china human rights dialogue. therefore, we welcome the fact that the most recent dialogue which was held in october in beijing allowed a sincere and an in-depth exchange of views on all topics of our concern, with several of the discussions leading to follow-up activity. it is important to recognise that this dialogue provides an important forum where both parties can openly speak about their genuine concerns while contributing to a better understanding of our differences – and our differences remain notable. in this context we regret the chinese decision to withdraw from the human rights seminar in berlin over the participation of two ngos and that, for similar reasons, the seminar could not be held in beijing recently. we consider that civil society has a very important role to play and the seminar provides the appropriate forum for ngos to make their valuable contributions. i trust we are able to find a mutually agreed solution so that this important exercise will continue its successful path in the future, as underlined by the eu-china summit. let me close by saying that there are two more important human rights issues which we regularly raise with the chinese side as a matter of high priority. one is the ratification by china of the international covenant on civil and political rights and the other one is the release of those who were imprisoned at the time of the tiananmen square demonstrations or who later commemorated the 1989 events. decisive action on both sides would send a clear positive signal and would be highly welcome.

member of the commission. madam president, the proposed instrument on maintenance obligations seeks to improve the precarious situation of people who depend on maintenance to meet their everyday needs. in the european union, where people are increasingly mobile, maintenance creditors – especially children – should not face obstacles to recover money due to them, particularly when the debtor, such as a parent, leaves or has moved abroad. i would like to thank ms grabowska, as rapporteur, for the efforts she has made to give a voice to stakeholders such as non-governmental organisations assisting maintenance creditors during the very important public hearing on 11 september. we generally welcome ms grabowska’s report, which supports the proposal in its essential elements. i have just a few remarks on some proposed amendments. first of all, on the legal basis. we are of the opinion that the current instrument relates to family law. however, i understand parliament’s concerns, given the existing legal context. that is why we have invited the council, in a communication adopted at the same time as the proposed regulation, to decide – in accordance with article 67(2) of the treaty – that the present instrument be adopted according to the codecision procedure. that is my opinion, and i will continue to ask council to act on this invitation. concerning the other amendments on the rules on applicable law. last month, negotiations on a worldwide convention on maintenance obligations were finalised successfully at the hague conference on private international law. given the satisfactory results of the convention and the accompanying protocol on applicable law, the community and its member states would like to adhere to those international rules. consequently, the rules of the regulation and related amendments proposed should be revised in order to ensure consistency with the international rules. the report proposes allowing the courts to apply their own law when cases come before them and when this would accelerate the resolution of the dispute. while we recognise the concern to speed up litigation, we believe that the proposed solution does not allow for sufficient legal certainty, and there is the danger that it would not serve the interest of maintenance creditors, who should be protected by application of the same substantive law, regardless of which court is considering the case. finally, parliament is now voting on its report. an international legal context has become clear. i strongly hope this project will be resumed at full speed in 2008. i very much trust that the council will give it the highest priority in the coming months.
the rapporteur. madam president! i'll start with a thank you. i would like to thank the european commission very much for the 24 hours of cooperation at the working level. i would like to thank the libe committee and the shadow rapporteurs, and above all the juri committee, the legal affairs committee and the rapporteur, mrs wallis, for their really excellent cooperation and for the fact that they also took on a great deal of the burden of convincing the commission of the proposals to change the legal basis. i shall begin with the legal basis, perhaps, because the fact is that we have received this regulation for adoption under a procedure which parliament could not accept. we wanted to propose a codecision procedure, not a consultation procedure. i am therefore pleased to hear the commissioner say that he is aware of the proposal to the council to open up this way of doing things. i would add one thing to what the commissioner said. the fact that the maintenance relationship is derived from family law, i don't question that. i think that it is mixed in its entirety, because the fact that it begins in family law does not mean that it continues in family law. its consequences are linked to the common market, to the economic situation, to the economic situation of both parties: of who is a maintenance debtor and of who is a creditor. we can therefore separate the maintenance relationship from family law and link the maintenance payments not to family law, which is really a matter for the member states, but to what parliament feels it is competent to do, namely the common market, care for the family, human rights, and then i think there should be no problem for this change in procedure to take place. i therefore believe that this proposal merits not only consideration but also acceptance by the council. we actually did, in preparing this regulation, have a hearing that was basically one big wall of tears. mostly women spoke about the difficulty they face in enforcing child support for children whose other parent is outside their country and who does not seem to be very interested in raising or putting up with the child. there are many tricks, and i'm not going to list them here, i'm just going to talk about one situation. all you have to do is change the letter in your name to die in europe and be almost untraceable, and then the child support obligation is gone. with this regulation, we would like to ensure that no debtor in europe, no debtor in alimony, feels safe, that he does not think that leaving his country, where he has a child who is not dependent on alimony, that he does not think that leaving in an open european union, with internal borders abolished, especially now that new countries are joining the schengen system in a few days, that this situation works in favour of those who do not take responsibility for their family. i would like to mention two aspects of the regulation which i consider to be the most important, two changes which are new, namely that a maintenance judgment given in the state where the person entitled is normally located will not have to be confirmed in the state where the maintenance debtor is present. the regulation proposes to abolish the "execution of maintenance". i know it's new, but if we want to ensure the effectiveness of the enforcement of maintenance, we have to decide. if we stop enforcement, then the whole initiative of more efficient enforcement of alimony is simply unattainable. i am aware that we will respect all the agreements reached in the framework of the hague convention and conference, but the international system is developing very slowly, it takes a long time, the ratification of agreements on private international law sometimes takes years. the union must move forward, must give children security when fathers or mothers have forgotten them. i therefore believe that this regulation needs to be implemented quickly for the sake of children. it not only protects the children but also the debtor. i therefore thank the portuguese presidency for the work it has put into its preparation and i place it in the hands of the slovenian presidency with full confidence that it will complete the text and that we will have a good regulation.

mr. chairman, please! unfortunately, the increasing number of divorces, combined with the increased mobility of eu citizens, is inevitably leading to an increasing number of cross-border child support disputes. at present, in order to enforce a claim against a so-called maintenance debtor residing in another member state, it is necessary to refer the matter to the courts of the state in which the judgment is to be enforced. unfortunately, this solution is often ineffective and it has become clear that there is a real need to establish specific rules on the jurisdiction of the court in matters relating to maintenance. the draft regulation aims to reduce the formal requirements for judicial decisions to be issued and enforced in each member state and to ensure effective enforcement. the new regulation, once it has entered into force, is intended to enable the person entitled to obtain an enforceable title valid throughout the european union, while simplifying and harmonising the system of enforcement. i welcome the action taken at the hague conference on private international law, but i fully agree with the rapporteur that the regulations in this area in the european union should be more advanced and, moreover, implemented more quickly. increasing mobility of citizens is leading to an increase in the number of international marriages where the spouses have different nationalities, live in different countries or live in a member state of which they are not both nationals. when an international couple decides to divorce, different legal provisions can therefore be invoked. the wide scope of the regulation is reflected in the alarmingly low level of maintenance payments in some eu countries - in my own country, poland, for example, only 10%. the draft law provides, inter alia, for the introduction of a right of the mother of a child born out of wedlock to have the father of the child pay the costs of pregnancy and childbirth and the costs of maintaining the mother during childbirth. currently, in many member states, this claim often does not qualify as a maintenance claim, which makes it much more difficult to pursue. before my country joined the european union, the courts handled over a thousand applications for maintenance claims abroad each year. as a consequence of the opening of the borders, all the forecasts predict a drastic increase in these claims, also in other countries. open borders and open labor markets may even cause some fathers to run away from child support. the children will suffer the most. we can't agree to that.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i will be very brief, but i thank all those who have spoken, the rapporteur, the other honourable members who have collaborated in this work. i believe that in the coming months we will have three objectives before us, which i hope the slovenian presidency will be able to carry out successfully. the first: the council must be convinced that if we support the usefulness of an amendment to article 67 of the treaty on a legal basis, we are doing so to give a stronger democratic basis to an initiative which objectively protects vulnerable groups of people, particularly children, following the breakdown of the family unit. the second objective is to ensure that the protection afforded to the creditor, irrespective of where the court is seised of a case, is similar: it would be very strange if the lex fori test led to a variation in the substantial protection of the creditor. so trying to harmonize the rules is another essential objective. the third objective, which i think we need to work on, is the actual implementation: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this does not work for maintenance obligations, because if it does, the provision will be void of meaning. we have made some rather innovative proposals: the temporary freezing of a part of the debtor's bank account if the debtor does not want to pay, or a periodic enforcement obligation on the assets, in respect of the amount that the debtor must pay. as you know, the member states in the council, by a large majority, have shown dissent and opposition, because this is the real part that makes a difference in a rule: either the order is enforceable, or there is no point in continuing to stress the importance of protecting the child or the separated spouse who is a maintenance creditor! the author. madam president! saudi arabia is a country where the law is enforced by wahhabi principles, the most radical sunni branch of islam. political, social and religious freedom is severely restricted, and flogging, amputation of arms and legs, and the death penalty are all routine. in a country that human rights watch calls a "human rights wasteland", women are the first to suffer from multiple forms of discrimination in their private and public lives. it was not until 2001 that the women's identities were formally recognised by issuing photo ids. previously, they used a family id card with a picture of the husband or father. even though they can afford a car, they're not allowed to drive it. they can study, but the male lecturer is on video. they're denied the right to vote, and divorce and child custody are the sole responsibility of the man. women are frequently the victims of unjust and degrading court decisions. the qatif girl case is a case of a 19-year-old gang rape victim who was sentenced to 200 lashes and six months in prison for being alone with a stranger at the time of her abduction. despite being a signatory, saudi arabia does not comply with its obligations under the convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women. the authorities must first remove restrictions on women's freedom of movement and take steps to progressively increase women's participation in political decision-making on an equal footing with men. women must have universal access to employment at all levels of government and to all public functions. furthermore, a total ban on the use of whipping and other humiliating corporal punishments should be demanded, as this constitutes a violation of international law and the un convention against torture, to which saudi arabia is a party.
the author, madam president! when we talk about crimes and when we think about the crimes of the 20th century, we think primarily of german crimes and bolshevik crimes, or rather, more broadly, communist crimes. in europe, we are less aware that in the far east, japan committed enormous crimes from the 1930s until the end of the war. among these crimes, one of the most serious was the sexual abuse of women during this time. about 100,000 women from conquered countries in the far east were forced into sexual slavery by the japanese imperial army. this sexual slavery, criminal in its own right, had even more consequences. the consequences were forced abortions, many mutilations, murders and many suicides of these women. of course, today, the women who are still alive are older and elderly. admittedly, the japanese government did much to compensate women for the terrible injuries they suffered during the postwar period. today, this resolution calls on the japanese government to make a final political, moral and financial settlement with these women who are still alive and with the families of those who are no longer alive. they really deserve it.
the commission notes that the commission has not provided any information on the number of companies that have been granted the aid. - madam president! - i have to go. today's debate is about the human rights violations that occurred in the 1930s and during the japanese occupation, where young women in the imperial military were sexually abused and forced into prostitution, despite the japanese government signing international conventions to combat the trafficking of women and children and supporting the un resolution on women, peace and security. the japanese prime minister's genuine regret is currently being questioned by japanese officials because the asian women's fund ended its program and mandate in march 2007, with only monetary compensation being paid to women. in supporting the resolution and the need for redress, we point out that the line between the norm and the pathology is blurred today too, which is in clear contradiction with moral norms, and therefore there is a need to radically combat prostitution as a form of modern slavery. prostitutes are not only victims of wars 50 years ago, but women are also exploited today, as in the belgian congo, as reported in the press, as well as in many other countries, even rich ones. in the name of respect for the human person, we should also expose the spread of a hedonistic and commercial culture that encourages sexual abuse, drawing even very young women and girls into prostitution and other forms of depravity. respect for the identity and dignity of women does not only consist in exposing crimes or abuses of sexual discrimination or other injustices, but above all in developing programmes and implementing principles covering all areas of women's lives, which should be based on a renewed awareness of the dignity of women as wives, mothers, carers or workers, as human beings, as equal to men, although not the same.
mr. chairman, please! on 13 december, the leaders of the european union countries signed the treaty of lisbon, which was renamed the european constitution. unfortunately, the signatories didn't know what they were signing, they didn't know because there is no consolidated version. the treaty has a piece of reference to some other document, and there again references. it's deliberately so complicated that no one can figure out what's inside. it concludes with 25 pages of explanations showing in three columns the relationship between the numbering of the articles of the old treaty, the provisional numbering in the lisbon treaty and the numbering that will be after the consolidated version is completed - total chaos. portugal, are you not ashamed to call such an unfinished document the treaty of lisbon? portugal, are you not ashamed to accept in such a humiliating way the schedule imposed by the german presidency as part of unification? portugal, are you not ashamed of deceiving the europeans by offering them to accept what they do not want, which they would surely reject in referendums, which they have already rejected? portugal, shame on you!
mr. chairman, please! i would first like to express my appreciation to the portuguese presidency and to mr josé sócrates for having led to the signing of the treaty of lisbon. this is a great achievement for europe, a very important, historic moment after years of deep crisis in the european union. at the same time, all eu member states must ratify the treaty by the end of the year. it will not be easy. we are witnessing the cynical use of the instruments of direct democracy against european democracy. i do not hesitate to say that those who today are cynical about the institution of the referendum are not doing so in good faith. we saw this last week in strasbourg, when all kinds of extremists on the european political scene raised the slogan of a referendum, which is in itself something of value, against the european treaty, and really against the european system of liberal democracy. mr. chairman, i also wanted to say something very personal today. 25 years ago in eastern europe we raised the slogan of a europe without borders against dictatorships in our countries. today, this week, europe is indeed becoming a continent without borders, the european union in a symbolic, technical and organisational sense. this is a great moment for the societies of the european union.
